Course_Title:
This course introduces the fundamentals of stress, strain, and constitutive re-
lations, followed by the governing equations of elasticity with applications to
plane stress and plane strain problems. The course emphasizes the analysis
of slender, thin-walled, and stiffened structures typical of aerospace systems,
including beams and wing-box type configurations. Topics include bending
of symmetric and unsymmetric sections, shear flow in open and closed thin-
walled sections, shear center determination, and deflection analysis. Torsion of
circular and noncircular members, including single- and multi-cell thin-walled
sections, is treated in detail, along with combined bending–torsion, behavior
under realistic loading conditions. The effects of temperature, material non-
homogeneity, and modulus-weighted sectional properties are also considered.
Structural stability through Euler buckling, as well as appropriate failure the-
ories, are introduced to assess safety and performance. The course ultimately
equips students with analytical and practical tools for modeling, analyzing,
and designing efficient aerospace structural components. A general overview
of measurement techniques and materials used in aerospace engineering will
also be covered in this course. Processing techniques for aerospace materials
and the criteria for material selection are also covered next. .

Course_Title:
This course focuses on the performance analysis of airplanes using fundamen-
tal principles of flight mechanics. It covers atmospheric models, drag polar
estimation, and engine performance characteristics, along with detailed anal-
ysis of steady and accelerated flight, climb, range, and endurance. The course
also includes aircraft manoeuvres, flight limitations, and take-off and land-
ing performance. Overall, it equips students with the ability to evaluate and
predict aircraft performance across different flight conditions

Course_Title:
The Propulsion I & II courses introduces the fundamental principles of
aerospace propulsion, with emphasis on air-breathing engines in two courses.
It covers thermodynamic cycle analysis, performance parameters such as
thrust and efficiency, and the working principles of turbojet, turbofan, turbo-
prop, and turboshaft engines. The course also includes introductory concepts
of ramjet and scramjet propulsion. Overall, it provides a strong foundation
for understanding propulsion system performance and energy conversion in
aerospace applications. The detailed analysis and design of propulsion system
components, particularly turbomachinery and combustion systems will also
be covered in this course. It covers the working principles and performance of
compressors and turbines, including stage dynamics, efficiency, and loss mech-
anisms. The course also addresses compressor–turbine matching, combustion
processes, and afterburners in gas turbine engines. Overall, it equips students
with the analytical and design skills required for advanced propulsion system
development.

Course_Title:
This course provides a comprehensive understanding of the three fundamen-
tal modes of heat transfer: conduction, convection, and radiation. It covers
both theoretical foundations and practical applications, including steady and
transient conduction, empirical correlations in convection, radiation exchange
mechanisms and principles of mass transfer. The course also introduces heat
exchanger analysis and design methodologies. Overall, it equips students with
the analytical skills required to solve real-world thermal engineering problems.

Course_Title:
The Aircraft Design course provides a comprehensive understanding of the
aircraft design process, from mission requirements to preliminary confgiura-
tion and sizing. It covers conceptual design, aerodynamic analysis, weight
estimation, and performance evaluation, along with stability and control con-
siderations. The course also introduces structural design principles, including
load estimation and stress analysis of aircraft components. Overall, it equips
students with the ability to integrate multidisciplinary aspects into a coherent
aircraft design framework using modern computational tools.

Course_Title:
The Control of Mechanical Systems course introduces the modeling, analysis,
and control of dynamic systems using classical control theory. It covers system
representation techniques, time and frequency response analysis, and stabil-
ity concepts such as BIBO and Routh criteria. The course further includes
controller design methods, including root locus and PID control, along with
practical implementation aspects. Overall, it equips students with the skills
to design and analyze control systems for real-world mechanical applications.

Course_Title:
The Aerospace Systems Engineering course provides a structured framework
for the analysis, design, and integration of complex aerospace systems. It em-
phasizes requirement definition, system architecture development, and model-
based systems engineering to support informed design decisions. The course
also covers trade-off analysis, system integration, verification, and risk assess-
ment across the system lifecycle. It enables students to develop multidis-
ciplinary problem-solving skills aligned with industry practices in aerospace
system design and development.

Course_Title:
Objective:
1. Equip students with an understanding of mathematical tools (vector calculus, linear algebra, complex
analysis, differential equations) and their application in modelling and solving engineering systems
2. Introduce concepts of probability and statistics essential in analyzing and interpreting data.
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Apply vector calculus, tensor analysis, matrix operations, probability and complex analysis concepts while
addressing engineering problems involving multivariable systems,
2. To understand methods to solve ODEs and PDEs in contexts like vibrations and heat transfer problems.
3. To effectively use statistical and numerical methods to analyzing experimental data, conduct hypothesis
testing, and solve engineering problems.
Contents:
1. Vectors, Tensors and Linear Algebra [7 lectures]:
Tensor notation and transformation. Matrix operations; LU factorization; Reduced row echelon form and
rank; Independence, Basis & dimension; Orthogonality, projection and least square approximation;
Determinant properties; Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors, Examples from Aerospace applications.
2. Second-order linear ODEs, System of ODEs,
series solutions of ODEs; Laplace transforms; Fourier series, Fourier transform, Example of Mass-Spring
System with Free and Forced vibration.
3. Complex Analysis [7 lectures]: Complex Numbers. Complex Plane, Analytic Function, Cauchy-Riemann
Equations. Laplace's Equation, Exponential Function, Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions, Line
Integral in the Complex Plane, Cauchy's Integral Theorem and Formula, conformal mappings and
examples.
4. Partial Differential Equations [6 lectures]: Characterization of PDEs, Separation of Variables for Partial
Differential Equations.
5. Numerical Ordinary differential equations ( 4 lectures]: -Kutta
Method, Integrating Higher order ODE using system of ODEs, Boundary value problem using shooting
method.
6. Probability and Statistics [8 lectures]: Probability and random variables, Central limit theorem and
Probability distributions, distributions of several random variables, random sampling, point estimation and
confidence intervals, Goodness of fit, regression, correlations

Course_Title:
Learning objectives: The objectives of this course are to:
1. Develop a fundamental understanding of aerospace materials, their properties, processing methods,
and performance in structural applications.
2. Analyze aerospace structures by understanding load paths, stress distribution, and structural behavior
under different loading conditions.
3. Apply concepts of material selection, structural design, and failure analysis for safe and efficient
aerospace systems.
Learning outcomes: After completing this course, students will be able to:
1. Evaluate the behavior and performance of aerospace materials based on mechanical properties,
processing, and environmental effects.
2. Analyze aerospace structural components by applying load, stress, and deformation principles.
3. Assess structural integrity through design considerations, failure mechanisms, joints, and durability
concepts.
Course Content:
1. Introduction to aerospace materials & processing [7 Lectures]: Overview of aerospace materials
and properties, selection of materials, Processing of metals, alloys, and polymers, FRP composites,
composites manufacturing, sandwich structures
2. Material performance, failure and testing [8 Lectures]: Mechanical testing of aerospace materials,
failure theories, fracture mechanics and crack propagation, fatigue behavior, environmental
degradation, brief of non-destructive testing (NDT)
3. Aerospace structural concepts and configurations [8 Lectures] : A brief history of aircraft and
spacecraft structures, airframe components, stress-strain concept in structural components, torsion of
thin wall structures with single and multiple cell, bending and shear forces, shear centre in thin-walled
structures, skin-stringer idealisation of fuselage and wing structures,
4. Loads, stress analysis and aerospace structural performance [8 Lectures]: Energy methods,
aircraft and spacecraft loads and load transfer mechanisms, torsional loading of fuselage, bending of
wing structures, buckling of column and plates, selection of design criteria.
5. Aerospace structural design, failure and joints [8 Lectures]: Design philosophy and approach,
safety, regulations, and standard certification requirements, design for fatigue and crack growth,
structural joints, durability and lifecycle considerations, AI/ML applications for structural design.

Course_Title:
Course Objectives
1. To develop a strong understanding of the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight mechanics,
aerodynamics, and performance.
2. To analyze aircraft motion, stability, control, and maneuvering characteristics under various flight
conditions.
3. To apply theoretical and computational methods for evaluating aircraft performance parameters such
as takeoff, landing, climb, range, endurance, and flight stability.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Calculate and evaluate key aircraft performance metrics including lift, drag, thrust requirements,
climb performance, range, and endurance.
2. Analyze static and dynamic stability characteristics of aircraft and explain the influence of control
surfaces and aerodynamic design parameters.
3. Apply flight mechanics principles and equations of motion to solve practical aerospace engineering
problems using analytical or simulation tools.
Contents:
1. Introduction [5 Lectures]: Aircraft types, Atmosphere properties, basics aerodynamic parameters
2. Aircraft Geometry and Aerodynamic forces [10 Lectures]: Aircraft geometry and coordinates
systems, Aerodynamic coefficients, Dynamic pressure, non-dimensional parameter. Lift generation,
lift curve, Drag Components (parasite, induced and wave drag), drag polar, minimum drag condition,
High lift devices (flaps, slats, leading-edge devices), lift augmentation and effect on take-off and
landing.
3. Equations of Motions [5 Lectures]: Fundamentals of aircraft motions, Aircraft equations of motion,
Steady flight level, Climbing and descending flight
4. Aircraft performance [11 Lectures]: Performance of Take-off( Ground roll, Rotation and lift-off,
balanced field length), Landing(Approach and flare, landing distance, Braking effect, reverse thrust),
Turning flight and maneuvering, Performance envelops (flight envelope , v-n diagram, stall boundaries,
operational limit), range and endurance(Breguet range equation, Fuel consumption, Jet aircraft range,
Propeller aircraft endurance, Payload-range tradeoff)
5. Supersonic flight basics [8 Lectures]: Compressibility effects, Shock waves, Critical Mach number,
Area rule, Supersonic drag rise.

Course_Title:
Course Objectives
1. Provide a foundational exposure to high-speed aerodynamics, highlighting physical phenomena
arising in compressible flows such as density variation, wave propagation, and compressibility
effects.
2. Build analytical understanding of flow features unique to supersonic regimes, including shock
formation, expansion processes, and their influence on aerodynamic performance.
3. Familiarize students with practical high-speed flow applications and introduce basic experimental
and visualization approaches used in supersonic wind tunnel studies.
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Estimate flow properties in high-speed regimes using appropriate compressible flow relations and
simplified models.
2. Interpret fundamental flow features such as shock waves and expansion fans in canonical
configurations (e.g., wedges, nozzles, and airfoils).
3. Relate high-speed flow concepts to engineering systems such as aircraft, propulsion devices, and
external aerodynamic configurations.
Contents
1. Introduction [4 Lectures]: Review of thermodynamics; Definition of Compressible flows,
Conservation equations for Inviscid flows.
2. Isentropic Flows [6 Lectures]: Speed of sound and Mach number, Wave propagation, Static and
stagnation conditions, isentropic flows with area change, isentropic nozzle operation; Prandtl-Meyer
expansion flows: Prandtl-Meyer function.
3. Non-Isentropic Flows-Normal and Oblique Shock Theory [7 Lectures]: Normal shock relations,
Rankine-Hugoniot equations.; 2-D flow equations, Oblique shock relations, Oblique shock chart,
Shock reflections, Regular reflections and Mach reflections, Shock Polar, Conical shock flows
4. Adiabatic flow with area change [5 Lectures]: Normal shock in c-d nozzles, oblique shocks in
overexpanded and under expanded nozzle flows.
5. Compressible flow with friction (Fanno Flow)/ Heat Transfer (Rayleigh flow) [7 lectures]:
Fanno Flow: Working equations, Fanno line and friction choking, Correlations with shock; Rayleigh
flow: Working equations, Rayleigh line and Thermal choking, Correlations with shock wave.
6. Unsteady compressible flows [4 Lectures]: 1-D wave motion: simple and finite waves, Riemann
invariants, wave propagation in shock tube, Moving shock relations, blast waves;
7. High-Speed Aerodynamics and Measurements in Compressible Flows [6 Lectures]: Prandtl-
Glauert rule, Aerodynamic design for High Speeds Critical Mach Number, Supercritical Aerofoils,
Swept Wings, Area Rule,

Course_Title:
PART A: Aerodynamics Lab
Course Objectives: To develop the ability to relate theoretical flow concepts in low-speed and high-speed
aerodynamics with experimentally observed flow features in internal and external flows.
1. To train students with lift and drag measurements in airfoils.
2. To train students in high-speed flow diagnostics, including pressure-based measurements and optical
visualization techniques.
3. To introduce students to steady and unsteady shock phenomena and their relevance in practical
aerodynamic and propulsion systems.
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Identify and interpret key flow features such as, lift coefficient, drag coefficient, choking, shock waves,
expansion fans, and jet structures from experimental observations.
2. Measure and compute flow properties (Mach number, pressure ratios, mass flow rate) using standard
diagnostic techniques in compressible flows.
3. Correlate experimental data with theoretical predictions for isentropic flows, normal/oblique shocks,
and nozzle flow behavior.
Laboratory Experiments
1. Measurement of surface pressure coefficients over an aerofoil and estimation of lift characteristics.
2. Measurement of aerodynamic coefficients using a force balance system
3. Prediction of choking point and mass flux variation in a convergent nozzle with a change in back
pressure.
4. Mach number prediction in supersonic flow using Pitot tube pressure measurement.
5. Schlieren and Shadowgraph optical flow visualization techniques for shock wave visualization.
6. Evaluating convergent-divergent (c-d) nozzle flow pressure curve and finding critical pressure ratios.
7. Prediction of normal shock location in c-d nozzle for various pressure ratios.
8. Oblique shock wave angle prediction with variation in flow deflection angle.

Course_Title:
Course Objective
1. To introduce the fundamentals of finite element analysis for one-dimensional engineering
problems and develop finite element formulations from governing differential equations,
2. To provide hands-on experience in MATLAB/Python-based FEM implementation and
validation using commercial simulation software.
Learning Outcomes
1. Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to formulate and solve one-
dimensional structural, thermal, and vibration problems using finite element methods.
2. Students will also be able to implement FEM algorithms computationally and validate
numerical results with analytical and commercial software solutions.
Contents
1. Introduction [3 Lectures]: Historical development and scope of FEM, General steps involved
in FEM, Applications, and advantages. Comparison of FE and exact solutions, Matrix notation,
treatment of boundary conditions, and solution for the unknown degree of freedom. Matlab
implementation.
2. Finite element formulation from governing differential equation [8 Lectures]: Weighted
residual method, Use of single continuous trial function. General weighted residual statement.
Weak (variational) form of the weighted residual statement. Comparison of differential
equation, weighted residual and weak forms. Piecewise continuous trial function solution of
the weak form. Rayleigh-Ritz Method, collocation method, Least square method, Galerkin
approach.
3. Finite Element Formulation for One-Dimensional Problems [10 Lectures]: Local
approximation function and global approximation function, convergence, continuity, and
completeness. Compatibility. Weak form for bar with varying cross-section, 1D linear and
higher order shape functions, Discrete equation, Local and global stiffness matrix, force vector
from weak form. Numerical integration, Gauss quadrature, transformation from physical space
to parent space. Matlab implementation. Verification with analytical solutions. Patch test.
4. FE-formulation for Beam elements [5 Lectures]: Beam theory, governing differential
equation and boundary conditions, Weak formulation, Hermite shape function, Derivation of
local stiffness matrix, and Force vector. Matlab implementation. Verification with analytical
solutions.
5. Finite element analysis of time-dependent problems [5 Lectures]: Transient heat
conduction equation, Weak formulation, FE-formulation. Finite difference approximation for
time. Explicit and implicit schemes. MATLAB/Python implementation of transient heat
conduction problems.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. Provide basic concept of space missions and role of launch vehicles and spacecraft in such missions,
including their trajectory, configuration and orbital/re-entry solutions.
Learning Outcomes
1. Formulate a realistic space mission starting from mission objectives
2. Arrive at the configuration of the applicable launch system and its ascent trajectory
3. Obtain the orbital / inter-planetary trajectory of spacecraft including their re-entry solutions

1. Introduction [3 Lectures]: Space missions, definitions and role of ascent, orbital, inter-planetary and
re-entry missions.

force models, General governing equations of ascent mission
3. Ascent Trajectory Analysis [7 Lectures]: Ideal motion solution, Rectilinear motion under gravity and

4. Launch Vehicle Design [4 Lectures]: Launch vehicle sizing for a mission, Multi-stage vehicle concept

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
Provide the basics of material and energy balances for Chemical Engineers.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to:
1. Gain basic understanding of material and energy balances.
2. Gain knowledge of applying the material and energy balances to Chemical Engineering Systems.

Introduction: Units and dimensions in chemical engineering (1 lecture), stoichiometric and
composition relations (1.5 lectures), concept of degrees of freedom and linear dependence of a
set of equations (1.5 lectures). [4 lectures]

with and without chemical reactions, material balance involving gases (5 lectures), vapors, liquids

determination of temperatures for adiabatic and non-adiabatic reactions (3 lectures). [13 lectures]
Simultaneous Material and Energy Balances: Degrees of freedom analysis for multicomponent
systems (2 lectures), combined steady state material and energy balances for units with multiple
sub-systems (2 lectures). [4 lectures]
Unsteady State Material and Energy Balances: Transient material and energy balances with and
without chemical reactions. [4 lectures]

Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will
● provide a rigorous and comprehensive foundation in the fundamental laws governing fluid flow.
● help the students understand the importance and application of fluid mechanics.
● exemplify concepts of similarity and model testing.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
● understand and apply the fundamental principles of fluid statics, kinematics, and dynamics to analyse
forces, pressures, and flow conditions in civil engineering systems
● derive and apply the governing equations of fluid motion to solve engineering problems
● design physical hydraulic models, interpret experimental results, and extend findings to prototype-scale
engineering predictions.
Contents
Introduction [3 Lecture]: Definition and properties of fluid, Newtonian and Non-Newtonian Fluids, Dimensions
and units, Continuum Hypothesis, Knudsen Number, Capillary and surface tension.
Pressure and Fluid Statics [5 Lectures]: Pascal’s Law, Manometry, hydrostatic force on submerged planar and
curved surfaces, buoyancy and stability, rigid body motion.
Fluid Kinematics [5 Lectures]: Graphical Description of Fluid Flow, Vorticity, Circulation, Stream and Potential
Functions, rotational-irrotational flows, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications.
Fluid Dynamics [9 Lectures]: Reynold Transport Theorem, Acceleration of fluid, Deformations in fluid particles,
derivation of Euler’s equation and Navier-Stokes equations.
Internal flow [6 Lectures]: Reynolds number regimes and Reynold experiments, Laminar and Turbulent flow in
pipes, Head Losses in pipes, Flow measurement in pipes, Pipe network analysis, Introduction of water hammer
effect and cavitation, Moody’s chart.
External flow [6 Lecture]: Boundary layer over flat plate, boundary layer thickness, Prandtl-boundary layer
equations, momentum integral equation, pressure gradient & separation, drag coefficients.
Dimensional analysis and similarity [2 Lectures]: Dimensionless Numbers, Scale and Similitude, Buckingham
Pi theorem and examples.
Flow in Open Channel [3 Lecture]: Discharge in open channel, Concept of Specific Energy and Alternate Depths,
Hydraulic Jump.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. Provide a basis understanding of material science.
2. Introduce students to the relationship between structure, properties, processing, and
performance of materials, for building a foundation for advance materials study.
Learning Outcomes
1- Explain the fundamental concepts of materials science, including the relationship between structure,
properties, processing, and performance.
Contents
Fundamental of material science [3 lectures]: Introduction to Materials Science & Engineering, Classification
of materials (metals, ceramics, polymers, composites), Structure–Property–Processing–Performance
relationship, Overview of advanced materials.
Atomic structure, Bonding & Crystal structure [6 lectures]: Atomic structure and electronic configuration,
Bonding force and energies, Ionic bonding, Covalent Bonding, Metallic Bonding. Crystal systems and Bravais
lattices, Miller indices (planes and directions), X-ray diffraction and Bragg’s law
Imperfections in Solids [5 lectures]: Point defects, Line defects and dislocations, Interfacial defects, Bulk or
volume defects, significance of defects in materials. Grain boundaries.
Mechanical Properties of Materials [5 lectures]: Concept of stress and Strain, Elastic deformation, Plastic
deformation, Shear, Hardness
Electrical properties of materials [5 lectures]: Electrical conduction in solids, Drift velocity, Energy bands:
valence band and conduction band, Intrinsic semiconductors, Extrinsic semiconductors. Diodes, Transistors, Solar
cells, Ferroelectricity, Piezoelectricity, Solar cell.
Magnetic properties of materials [5 lectures]: Magnetic dipole moment, Electron spin, Diamagnetism,
Paramagnetic, Ferromagnetism, Antiferromagnetism, Ferrimagnetism, Domain structure, Hysteresis loop, soft vs
hard magnetic materials.
Optical properties of materials [5 lectures]: Reflection, refraction, absorption, transmission, Refractive index,
Band gap and color of materials, Light interaction with solids, Optical fibers.
Thermal properties of materials [5 lectures]: Basic laws of thermodynamics, specific heat, entropy, thermal
conductivity, thermal stresses.
Text Books
1. W. D. Callister Jr. and D. G. Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction,
10th ed. Hoboken, NJ, USA: John Wiley & Sons, 2020.
References
1. Raghavan, V. (2004). Materials science and engineering: A first course. Prentice Hall India.
Online Course Material
Massachusetts Institute of Technology. (2005). Fundamentals of Materials Science (3.012). MIT
OpenCourseWare. https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-012-fundamentals-of-materials-science-fall-2005/

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. Provide a basis for describing and understanding the stability of various forms of matter including metals,
polymers, and multi-phase systems.
2. Provide a basis for predicting the properties and phase behavior of equilibrated systems as a function of
their chemical content and interfacial characteristics.
Learning Outcomes
1. Establish the conditions for stability of a material and derive its properties.
2. Control the evolution of microstructures with respect to different thermal and compositional parameters.
Contents
Introduction to thermodynamics of materials [2 lectures]: Introduction – systems and boundaries, concept of
state, state and path functions, equilibrium definition, thermodynamics variables – extensive and intensive.
Laws of thermodynamics [10 lectures]: First law of thermodynamics, internal energy, heat capacity, adiabatic
processes, second law of thermodynamics, entropy and statistical interpretation of entropy, third law of
thermodynamics and thermodynamic functions: Helmholtz free energy, enthalpy, Gibbs free energy, chemical
potential, Maxwell’s relations, Gibbs-Helmholtz relation.
Single component systems [2 lectures]: Phase equilibrium in single component systems, Gibbs free energy
variation with pressure and temperature, P-T diagrams, Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
Behaviour of gases and solution thermodynamics [8 lectures]: Ideal and non-ideal gases, activity, fugacity,
partial molar quantities, Raoult’s law and Henry’s law, Gibbs-Duhem equation, Gibbs free energy of formation
of a solution (ideal, non-ideal), regular solution model, statistical model of solutions, Flory-Huggins theory and
Flory interaction parameter (𝝌), entropy of mixing for polymeric chains.
Composition and binary phase diagrams [8 lectures]: Thermodynamic activity, criterion for phase stability,
Gibbs free energy composition diagrams, activity-composition diagrams, application of regular solution model
to phase diagrams, Gibbs phase rule, phase behavior in polymer systems: LCST/UCST, phase separation in
polymer blends.
Surface and Interfacial Thermodynamics [4 lectures]: Adsorption and interphase: work of adhesion,
thermodynamics of fiber-matrix interfaces.
Reactions involving gases and condensed phase [5 lectures]: Reaction equilibrium a gas mixture and the
equilibrium constant, effect of pressure and temperature on the equilibrium constant, standard Gibbs free
energy variation with temperature, Ellingham diagrams, effect of phase transformations.

1. Gaskell, D.R. and Laughlin, D.E., (2018), Introduction to Thermodynamics of Materials, 6th Edition CRC
Press

Basis, Second edition, Cambridge University Press

Course_Title:
Objectives:
1. Introduce numerical methods and scientific-computing tools for solving materials-engineering
problems.
2. Enable students to analyze experimental and simulation data quantitatively and automate common
calculations.
Learning outcomes:
1. Read, process and visualize typical materials datasets.
2. Apply basic numerical methods to materials problems.
3. Implement small, reusable scripts for routine calculations and analyses.
Contents
Materials Data handling and mathematical foundations (7 lectures):Data handling and exploratory analysis -
Reading and organizing materials datasets, units, metadata. Descriptive statistics for experimental data. Basic
probability and statistics for engineering data. Vectors and matrices as data containers. Matrix operations.
Power series and Taylor series as local approximations to functions. Brief discussion of numerical error:
truncation vs round‑off. Fourier Transform and application on diffraction and FTIR spectroscopy
Curve fitting, regression, interpolation (9 lectures): Linear regression in one variable; analytical formula and
matrix form, General linear least squares, Polynomial regression, Overfitting vs underfitting, interpolation vs
regression, Polynomial interpolation, Runge phenomenon, Splines and piecewise interpolation, Brief idea of
Fourier, Nonlinear regression and model fitting on stress-strain, saturation growth, diffusion
Numerical differentiation and integration (9 lectures): Finite‑difference approximations: forward, backward,
central differences; order of accuracy. Differentiating discrete experimental data: slopes of stress–strain curves,
dD/dT for diffusion data, Sensitivity to noise; smoothing vs differentiation trade‑offs. Rectangle rule,
trapezoidal rule, Simpson’s 1/3 rule; error orders. Composite rules, non‑uniform grids; integrating experimental
data with uneven spacing.
Linear systems and eigenvalue (9 lectures): Solving linear systems, Formulating engineering problems as
Ax=b: mixture rules, force balance, simple thermal networks. Interpreting least‑squares regression as solver.
Rank deficiency and ill‑conditioning. Basic idea of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, modes and stability. Concept
of eigenvalues and eigenvectors relevant to diffusion and vibration.
Initial‑value ODEs and simple diffusion/thermal problems (5 lectures): ODEs – fundamentals and explicit
methods, Initial‑value problems with physical examples of cooling of a body, and simple kinetics. Euler’s
method and improved Euler. Runge–Kutta methods. Diffusion/heat-conduction in 1D.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. To inculcate fundamental concepts of stress, strain, and deformation of solids
2. Fundamentals of applying equilibrium, compatibility, and forced deformation relationships to structural
elements
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Apply the fundamentals to analyze structural members and gain physical insight into their stress and strain
distributions.
2. Ability to design structural members using dimensions, force-displacement relationships, boundary
conditions, loading, and allowable stress
Contents
Concept of stress [7 Lectures]: Surface and body forces, concept of stress at a point, stress equilibrium, plane
stress case: transformation of stresses at a point, principal stresses, and Mohr's circle, St. Venant’s principles.
Concept of strain [5 Lectures]: Displacement field, strain at a point, compatibility relations, volumetric
strain, plane strain case: transformation of strain at a point, principal strains and Mohr's circle, Strain Rosette;
Material behaviour and mathematical model [4 Lectures]: Concepts of elasticity, response of real materials,
Generalized Hooke's law (without and with thermal strains) for isotropic materials, orthotropic, and
anisotropic materials.
Application of Elasticity:
One-dimensional axial deformation [2 Lectures]: axial force diagram, basic relations for axial deformations,
Stress concentration.
Torsion of circular members [3 Lectures]: Basic relations for torsion of circular members, stress distribution
of torsion members.
Pressure Vessels [3 Lectures]: Thin-walled pressure vessel theory, thin-walled spheres, thin-walled
cylinders.
Beams [7 Lectures]: Shear force and moment diagrams; moment-curvature relationship for pure bending of
beams with symmetric cross-section; bending stress, shear stress; cases of combined stresses; deflection due
to bending.
Buckling [3 Lectures]: Concept of elastic instability, Introduction to column buckling, Euler's formula.
Energy methods [5 Lectures]: Concept of strain energy; strain energy for simple structural elements;
Castigliano's theorems; principle of minimum potential energy.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. To develop a fundamental understanding of kinetics in materials, focusing on diffusion, reaction rates,
interface phenomena, and microstructural evolution.
2. To enable application of these principles to analyze and apply kinetic principles to materials processing,
performance, and degradation across diverse material systems.
Learning Outcomes
1. Explain the fundamental concepts of kinetics, including driving forces, activation energy, and rate
processes in materials.
2. Interpret and analyze transport, reaction, and interface-controlled phenomena using appropriate kinetic
models and equations.
3. Apply kinetic principles to real materials processing scenarios such as sintering, additive manufacturing,
and environmental interactions.
Contents
Fundamentals of Kinetics [6 lectures]: Thermodynamics vs kinetics, driving force and atomic mobility, energy
barriers and activation energy, heterogeneous and homogeneous reactions, nucleation kinetics, overview of
rate processes in materials, rate equations and temperature dependence, Arrhenius equation.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. Identify the various forms of corrosion and their mechanisms.
2. Establish the thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers that govern metallic degradation.
3. Develop proficiency in using mixed potential theory to predict corrosion rates.
Learning Outcomes
1. Develop the understanding of basic electrochemical processes and redox reactions.
2. Design protection strategies using electrochemical methods, alloy selection, and advanced surface
coatings.
Contents
Introduction [3 lectures]: Corrosion – definition, different forms of environmental degradation, cost of
corrosion, electrochemical nature.
Thermodynamics of Corrosion [8 lectures]: Free energy and electrochemical potential – EMF series, Nernst
relationship, important reactions, cell potential, reference electrodes, Pourbaix diagram and its importance in
corrosion, construction of Pourbaix diagrams for Al, Cu, Fe, and Ni.
Kinetics of corrosion [6 lectures]: Current density and corrosion rate, corrosion rate expressions, exchange
current density, polarization – activation, concentration and resistance overpotential.
Mixed potential theory [9 lectures]: Mixed potential theory, applications to active metals, passivation,
application of mixed potential theory in passivating metals, understanding of corrosion on the basis of mixed
potential theory: activation controlled and concentration controlled corrosion.
Corrosion protection [4 lectures]: Cathodic protection, sacrificial anode and impressed current cathodic
protection (ICCP), anodic protection, industrial application and calculations, protection of metals and alloys,
coatings, inhibitors, materials selection/substitution.
Corrosion testing [3 lectures]: Immersion test, salt fog test, electrochemical work bench-3-electrode
electrochemical cells, reference electrode, counter electrode and potentiostat. Potentiodynamic test,
Galvanostatic test, linear polarization.
Stress effect on corrosion [3 lectures]: stress corrosion cracking (SCC), corrosion fatigue, hydrogen
embrittlement.
Thermodynamics of oxidation [3 lectures]: oxidation of metals and alloys, Pilling Bedworth ratio, Ellingham
diagram, kinetics of oxidation, effect of doping on the oxidation behavior.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. To build complete ML pipelines for materials problems: data preparation, featurization, model
selection, evaluation and interpretation.
2. To give hands-on experience with regression, classification and clustering for real materials datasets,
using the algorithms learned earlier in the institute ML course.
Learning Outcomes
Students will be able to
1. Construct and clean materials datasets and build appropriate feature sets (composition, structure,
microstructure, processing) and use unsupervised learning to explore materials spaces.
2. Train, validate and interpret ML models (regression and classification) for materials‑property
prediction and critically assess model performance, uncertainty for materials decisions.
Contents
Materials datasets and featurization (9 Lectures): Types of materials datasets; scalar, vector and image data.
Data cleaning: missing values, outliers, unit consistency; basic exploratory analysis. Compositional
descriptors: simple composition‑based features (averages, differences, moments of atomic properties);
introduction to established descriptor ideas at high level. Structural, microstructural and processing
descriptors: space group, lattice parameters, phase labels, grain size, phase fractions, texture indicators;
encoding process routes and heat‑treatment schedules.
Supervised learning for materials (7 Lectures): Problem formulation: targets, features, data splits
(train/validation/test), cross‑validation; avoiding data leakage. Regression tasks: using linear regression,
k‑NN, tree‑based models or simple ensembles to predict continuous properties. Classification tasks:
binary/multi‑class problems; metrics. Model selection and regularisation at an intuitive level.
Unsupervised learning and exploration (4 Lectures):Clustering: k‑means and/or another simple algorithm;
grouping alloys/ceramics into families based on descriptors. Dimensionality reduction: PCA for visualising
high‑dimensional descriptor spaces; interpreting principal components in materials terms.
Interpretation, reliability and small‑data issues (6 Lectures):Feature importance and simple sensitivity
analyses; interpreting learned relationships in the context of known materials science. Overfitting, domain of
applicability, uncertainty and robustness; pitfalls with small and biased materials datasets. Documentation
and reproducibility; basic good practices for datasets and models.
Deep Learning and Large Language Models for Materials Informatics (8 Lectures): Introduction to neural
networks: perceptron, shallow and deep neural networks; basic ideas of training, activation functions, and
backpropagation. Overview of deep learning architectures relevant to scientific and materials data.
Introduction to transformer models and large language models (LLMs)- embeddings, attention mechanism,
prompting, fine-tuning, and limitations of LLMs. Applications of LLMs in engineering and materials science,
including literature mining, materials-property prediction, workflow automation, scientific assistants, inverse
materials design, and autonomous laboratories.
Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) (5 Lectures): Introduction to MLIPs and their importance
in modern computational materials science. Descriptor concepts and representations for atomic environments.
Overview of neural-network interatomic potentials, Gaussian Approximation Potentials (GAP), Equivariant
Deep Descriptor Potentials (EDDPs)

Course_Title:
Objective:
1.​ To inculcate fundamental concepts of stress, strain, and deformation of solids
2.​ Fundamentals of applying equilibrium, compatibility, and forced deformation relationships to structural elements
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1.​ Apply the fundamentals to analyze structural members and gain physical insight into their stress and strain
distributions.
2.​ Ability to design structural members using dimensions, force-displacement relationships, boundary conditions,
loading, and allowable stress
Contents:
Concept of stress [7 Lectures]: Surface and body forces, concept of stress at a point, stress equilibrium, plane stress
case: transformation of stresses at a point, principal stresses, and Mohr's circle, St. Venant’s principles.
Concept of strain [5 Lectures]: Displacement field, strain at a point, compatibility relations, volumetric strain,
plane strain case: transformation of strain at a point, principal strains and Mohr's circle, Strain Rosette;
Material behaviour and mathematical model [4 Lectures]: Concepts of elasticity, response of real materials,
Generalized Hooke's law (without and with thermal strains) for isotropic materials, orthotropic, and anisotropic
materials.
Application of Elasticity:
One-dimensional axial deformation [2 Lectures]: axial force diagram, basic relations for axial deformations,
Stress concentration.
Torsion of circular members [3 Lectures]: Basic relations for torsion of circular members, stress distribution of
torsion members.
Pressure Vessels [3 Lectures]: Thin-walled pressure vessel theory, thin-walled spheres, thin-walled cylinders.
Beams [7 Lectures]: Shear force and moment diagrams; moment-curvature relationship for pure bending of beams
with symmetric cross-section; bending stress, shear stress; cases of combined stresses; deflection due to bending.
Buckling [3 Lectures]: Concept of elastic instability, Introduction to column buckling, Euler's formula.
Energy methods [5 Lectures]: Concept of strain energy; strain energy for simple structural elements; Castigliano's
theorems; principle of minimum potential energy.

Course_Title:
Objective:
1.​ To inculcate the fundamental laws governing fluid flow
2.​ Help the students to understand the importance and application of fluid mechanics

1.​ Apply fundamental knowledge in modelling and analysis of fluid flow problems in engineering
2.​ Interpret data from experiments of fluid flows and solve using differential equations and charts
Contents:

calculus and index notations
Fluid statics (5 Lectures): Basic equations, Manometry, Hydrostatic force on submerged bodies, rigid body
motion

Differential analysis (6 Lectures): Kinematics of fluids, deformations in fluid particle, strain rate, vorticity,
stream function, potential function, streamlines, pathlines, streaklines, derivation of Navier-Stokes equations

thickness, Prandtl-boundary layer equations, momentum integral equation, adverse pressure gradient &
separation, drag coefficients
Dimensional analysis and similarity (2 Lectures): Buckingham Pi theorem and examples
Introduction to turbulent flows (3 Lectures): Decomposition of instantaneous velocities, time-averaged
continuity and Navier-Stokes equations, Reynolds stresses, turbulent viscosity

Course_Title:
Objective: The objectives of the course are:
1.​ To develop the ability to formulate and solve engineering problems involving conduction, convection,
radiation and mass transfer.
2.​ To explain the design and performance analysis of fins, heat exchangers and thermal systems involving
phase change.
3.​ To introduce empirical correlations and heat-mass transfer analogies through practical engineering
applications.
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1.​ Analyze steady and transient conduction problems in plane walls, cylinders, spheres and extended surfaces.
2.​ Evaluate heat transfer coefficients for internal/external forced convection and natural convection using
appropriate correlations.
3.​ Analyze boiling, condensation, radiation exchange and heat exchanger performance using LMTD and
effectiveness-NTU methods.
4.​ Apply diffusion laws and heat-mass transfer analogies to solve basic mass transfer and simultaneous heat and
mass transfer problems.
Contents:
Introduction and basic concepts [1 Lectures]: Modes of heat transfer, Fourier’s law, thermal conductivity, thermal
diffusivity, convection coefficient, radiation heat exchange.
Heat conduction equation and boundary conditions [3 Lectures]: General heat conduction equation;
one-dimensional conduction in plane walls, cylinders and spheres; boundary and initial conditions; heat generation.
Steady heat conduction [4 Lectures]: Thermal resistance concept, network analysis, composite
walls/cylinders/spheres, thermal contact resistance, critical radius of insulation and heat transfer from fins.
Transient heat conduction [3 Lectures]: Lumped capacitance method, Biot and Fourier numbers, transient
conduction in large plane walls, long cylinders and spheres; semi-infinite solids.
Fundamentals of convection [3 Lectures]: Velocity and thermal boundary layers, laminar and turbulent flows,
conservation equations, non-dimensional numbers.
External forced convection [3 Lectures]: Drag and heat transfer in external flow, parallel flow over flat plates, flow
across cylinders and spheres.
Internal forced convection [4 Lectures]: Mean velocity and temperature, entrance region, hydrodynamic and
thermal entry lengths, laminar and turbulent tube flow, constant wall temperature/heat flux conditions and pressure
drop.
Natural/free convection [3 Lectures]: Physical mechanism, Grashof and Rayleigh numbers, natural convection
over plates, cylinders and spheres, enclosures, and mixed convection criteria.
Boiling and condensation [3 Lectures]: Boiling curve, pool boiling regimes, nucleate and film boiling, critical heat
flux, dropwise and film condensation, and Nusselt’s film condensation theory.
Heat exchangers [4 Lectures]: Types of heat exchangers, overall heat transfer coefficient, fouling factor, LMTD
method, correction factor, effectiveness-NTU method.
Thermal radiation and radiation exchange [5 Lectures]: Radiation laws, blackbody and gray-body radiation,
radiative properties, intensity, view factors, radiation exchange between black and diffuse-gray surfaces, radiation
shields and electrical network analogy.
Mass transfer [3 Lectures]: Heat-mass transfer analogy, Fick’s law, diffusion in stationary and moving media,
boundary conditions, steady and transient mass diffusion.

Course_Title:
Objectives
1.​ To familiarize students with methods to characterize the dynamical behaviour of mechanical systems using
mathematical models.
2.​ To provide an understanding of the fundamental concepts of control theory.
Learning Outcomes
1.​ Students will be able to develop mathematical models of mechanical systems and apply appropriate methods
for their representation and analysis.
2.​ Students will be able to design control systems for linear time-invariant (LTI) systems.
Contents
Introduction to Control [3 Lectures]: Control objectives; introduction to control problems; open- and closed-loop
control structures; properties of feedback systems; basic sensitivity analysis; effect of control gain on system
performance; effect of disturbances on tracking error.
Introduction to Modelling & Representation [6 Lectures]: Objectives; basic modelling concepts and types of
models; models of simple mechanical systems; linearization of nonlinear models; LTI systems; transfer function
and state-space modelling of LTI systems; conversion from state space to transfer function; block diagram
representation and manipulation.
Response & Stability Analyses [5 Lectures]: Test signals; response of first- and second-order as well as
higher-order systems; poles and zeros and their effect on system response; stability criteria; BIBO stability; Routh’s
stability criterion.
Analysis of Feedback System [4 Lectures]: Basic control equation: stability, regulation, tracking, and sensitivity;
control of steady-state errors to polynomial inputs; system type and steady-state error; proportional (P), integral (I),
and derivative (D) control; PI and PID control; Ziegler–Nichols tuning of the PID controller.
Root Locus and Compensator Design [6 Lectures]: Concept of root locus; use of control gain to change pole
locations; design of lead, lag, and lead–lag compensators using root locus techniques.
Frequency Response Design Method [6 Lectures]: Frequency response and its representation using Bode and
Nyquist plots; Nyquist stability analysis; concepts of gain and phase crossover frequencies; gain and phase
margins; design of PD, PI, lead, lag, and PID compensators.
Design in State Space [5 Lectures]: Canonical forms of state equations; response from state equations; control law
design for full-state feedback; selection of poles; estimator design; combined control law and estimator.
Implementation of Control Law [2 Lectures]: Discretization of control law; difference equations; computational
aspects of control law.
Applications of Control to Mechanical Systems [2 Lectures]: Practical aspects of control
implementation—actuators and sensors; temperature control; flow control; pressure and force control; vehicle

Course_Title:
Objective: (a) To introduce the fundamentals of finite element analysis for one-dimensional engineering problems
and develop finite element formulations from governing differential equations, (b) To provide hands-on experience
in MATLAB/Python-based FEM implementation and validation using commercial simulation software.
Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to formulate and solve
one-dimensional structural, thermal, and vibration problems using finite element methods. Students will also be able
to implement FEM algorithms computationally and validate numerical results with analytical and commercial
software solutions.
Contents:
Introduction [3 Lectures]: Historical development and scope of FEM, General steps involved in FEM,
Applications, and advantages. Comparison of FE and exact solutions, Matrix notation, treatment of boundary
conditions, and solution for the unknown degree of freedom. Matlab implementation.
Finite element formulation from governing differential equation [8 Lectures]: Weighted residual method, Use of
single continuous trial function. General weighted residual statement. Weak (variational) form of the weighted
residual statement. Comparison of differential equation, weighted residual and weak forms. Piecewise continuous
trial function solution of the weak form. Rayleigh-Ritz Method, collocation method, Least square method, Galerkin
approach.
Finite Element Formulation for One-Dimensional Problems [10 Lectures]: Local approximation function and
global approximation function, convergence, continuity, and completeness. Compatibility. Weak form for bar with
varying cross-section, 1D linear and higher order shape functions, Discrete equation, Local and global stiffness
matrix, force vector from weak form. Numerical integration, Gauss quadrature, transformation from physical space
to parent space. Matlab implementation. Verification with analytical solutions. Patch test.
FE-formulation for Beam elements [5 Lectures]: Beam theory, governing differential equation and boundary
conditions, Weak formulation, Hermite shape function, Derivation of local stiffness matrix, and Force vector. Matlab
implementation. Verification with analytical solutions.
Finite element analysis of time-dependent problems [5 Lectures]: Transient heat conduction equation, Weak
formulation, FE-formulation. Finite difference approximation for time. Explicit and implicit schemes.
MATLAB/Python implementation of transient heat conduction problems.
Finite element analysis eigenvalue problems and structural dynamics [8 Lectures]: Introduction to eigenvalue
problems in engineering applications, free vibration of a rod, free vibration of a beam. Structural dynamics,
governing differential equations for a bar, including the inertia term. Weak formulation. FE-formulation. Consistent
mass matrix and Lumped mass matrix. Explicit and Implicit time integration scheme. Newmark’s method.
MATLAB/Python implementation of vibration problems.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will:
1.​ To develop fundamental understanding of stress, strain, plasticity, and material behavior relevant to metal
forming processes.
2.​ To analyze sheet metal deformation mechanisms, yielding behavior, formability, and instability during
various sheet forming operations.
3.​ To study the mechanics and applications of bending, deep drawing, stamping, and hydroforming processes
used in industrial sheet metal manufacturing.
Learning Outcomes
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
1.​ Apply concepts of stress–strain analysis, plastic deformation, and material properties to metal forming
problems.
2.​ Analyze sheet metal forming processes considering yielding, work hardening, formability, deformation
modes, and failure mechanisms.
3.​ Evaluate and design sheet metal operations such as bending, stamping, deep drawing, and hydroforming
with consideration of springback, instability, and forming limits.
Contents:
Introduction and Fundamentals of Metal Forming Mechanics [11 Lectures]: Introduction to the course: different
metal forming processes, importance of plasticity in the course. Review-Analysis of stress: transformation relations,
principal stresses and directions, maximum normal and shear stresses, invariants, hydrostatic and deviatoric parts;
Analysis of (infinitesimal) strain: transformation relations, principal strains, invariants, hydrostatic and deviatoric
parts; (Infinitesimal) rotation, Stress-strain relations for isotropic, linearly elastic material. Description of Material
properties: Introduction, Tensile test, Effect of properties on forming and formability.
Sheet Metal Forming and Plastic Deformation Analysis [14 Lectures]: Sheet deformation processes: Uni-axial
tension, general sheet forming processes, yielding, flow rule, work hardening hypothesis, work of plastic
deformation, isotropic yield functions, isotropic yield functions, effective stress and strain, Sheet deformation in
plane stress, strain distributions, strain diagram, deformation modes, effective stress-strain laws, principal tensions,
Stamping analysis: 2-D modeling of stamping, stretch and draw ratios in stamping.
Load instability and tearing: uniaxial tension of perfect strip and imperfect strip, tensile instability in stretching
continuous sheet, tensile instability in stretching continuous sheet.
Sheet Metal Formability, Bending and Deep Drawing [14 Lectures]: Sheet formability: Forming limit curve -
concept and evaluation, FLC, formability tests, theoretical prediction, factors affecting FLC, Sheet bending:
Variables in bending a continuous sheet, equilibrium conditions, material models, bending without tension,
springback prediction Cylindrical deep drawing & Stretching circular shells: Drawing the flange, cup height,
redrawing cylindrical cups, wall ironing of deep drawn cups, Analysis of bulging with fluid pressure, stretching over
punch, Hydroforming, Demonstration on sheet forming operations - stretching, bending, deep drawing.

Course_Title:
Objective: The objective of the course is to
1.​ provide a rigorous theoretical foundation in nonlinear continuum mechanics for the modeling and analysis of
deformable solids, developing a unified understanding of kinematics, stress, balance laws, and constitutive
principles with strong emphasis on physical consistency through objectivity, material symmetry, and
energy-based formulations.
2.​ bridge fundamental theory with practical engineering applications while preparing students for advanced
study and research in solid mechanics, computational mechanics, fracture, biomechanics, and related fields.
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1.​ Apply tensor and field-based tools to describe physical quantities and analyze deformation kinematics in
material and spatial frameworks.
2.​ Formulate stress and traction measures, apply balance laws in spatial and referential forms, and analyze stress
using invariants.
3.​ Develop objective, symmetry-consistent constitutive models and analyze finite deformation and nonlinear
elastic behavior through energy-based approaches.
Contents:
Mathematical Foundations [6 Lectures]: Scalars, vectors, and tensors; index notation; tensor products and
contractions; invariants; eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric tensors; change of basis and transformation laws;
scalar, vector, and tensor fields; differential operators.
Kinematics [8 Lectures]: Bodies and configurations; reference and current descriptions; motion, displacement,
velocity, and acceleration fields; material and spatial derivatives; deformation gradient; transformation of line, area,
and volume elements; polar decomposition; strain measures and linearized kinematics; velocity gradient, rate of
deformation, and spin tensor; rigid body motions and objectivity in kinematics.
Stress Measures and the Concept of Stress [6 Lectures]: Traction vectors and Cauchy’s postulate; existence and
interpretation of the Cauchy stress tensor; stress transformation, principal and extremal stresses, and stress invariants;
alternative stress measures including the first and second Piola-Kirchhoff stresses; physical interpretation through
representative stress states.
Mechanical Balance Laws and Field Equations [5 Lectures]: Conservation of mass; Reynolds transport theorem;
balance of linear and angular momentum; balance of mechanical energy.
Constitutive Principles and Objectivity [5 Lectures]: Constitutive response functions; material frame indifference
and change of observer; objective scalar, vector, and tensor fields; objective stress rates; material symmetry and
isotropy; linearization of constitutive laws.
Nonlinear Elasticity and Hyperelastic Materials [5 Lectures]: Hyperelastic material concept; strain energy density
functions; compressible and incompressible responses; classical hyperelastic models including Neo-Hookean,
Mooney Rivlin, Ogden, Gent, etc.
Applications [4 Lectures]: Homogeneous deformation of hyperelastic membranes under uniaxial and biaxial
loading, and simple shear; balloon inflation, instabilities of soft materials: snap through instability and morphological
instabilities: wrinkles, creases, folds, and ridges.

2.​ Jog, C.S., 2015. Continuum mechanics (Vol. 1). Cambridge University Press.

Course_Title:
Objective: The objective of the course is to
1.​ Provide the fundamentals of linear elastic fracture mechanics,
2.​ Introduce various numerical approaches for solving fracture problems.
Learning Outcomes: After completing this course, students will be able to
1.​ Solve fracture problems numerically using both discrete and diffuse approaches.
2.​ Interpret numerical results.
Contents
Background [3 Lectures]: Historical development, Review of crack-tip fields in linear elastic fracture mechanics
(LEFM); Modes of fracture (I, II, III), Analytical solution of plane crack problems, stress intensity factors, energy
release rate, and their equivalence.
Energy release rate [10 Lectures]: Griffith theory and extensions (Irwin, Orowan); Critical energy release rate;
R-curve behavior and fracture stability, concept of J-integral (path independence), Relation between G and J,
Introduction to elastic-plastic fracture mechanics (EPFM) parameters (CTOD, J as nonlinear energy release rate),
calculation of SIF (analytical, experimental, numerical methods).
Review of Finite Element Method [5 Lectures]: Basic concepts of FEM, weak formulation of boundary value
problems, discretization, interpolation functions, FE-formulation for scalar and vector valued problems, Assembly of
global equations, and solution procedure.
Discrete approach for fracture simulation [13 Lectures]: FE for the cracked body, Need for mesh refinement near
the crack tip, Singular and quarter-point elements, Method for determining fracture parameters, Domain and
interaction integral approach. Extended finite element method, enrichment functions: crack tip and heavyside
functions, Cohesive zone model.
Diffuse approach for fracture simulation [13 Lectures]: Introduction of various diffuse approaches, Phase-field
model for fracture, derivation of governing equations from variational principle, Length-scale parameter and
regularization; Phase-field for brittle fracture (AT model, phase-field evolution); Extensions to fatigue; Advantages
over discrete methods (no explicit crack tracking, natural branching/coalescence); Numerical implementation
(staggered/monolithic solvers).

Course_Title:
Objective: The objective is to
1.​ provides a rigorous theoretical foundation in the mechanics of smart materials and structures, focusing on
deformable systems governed by coupled mechanical, electrical, and magnetic fields.
2.​ Provide understanding of multiphysics coupling, structural response, and energy-based constitutive principles
grounded in thermodynamic consistency, work conjugacy, reciprocity, and stability.
Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to:
1.​ Apply continuum and field-based mechanics concepts to describe coupled mechanical, electrical, and
magnetic phenomena in deformable materials and structural systems.
2.​ Formulate and analyze energy-based constitutive relations for electromechanical and magnetomechanical
coupling, ensuring physical consistency through work conjugacy, reciprocity, and stability.
3.​ Model and assess smart structures incorporating active materials, architected geometries, and periodic media
for sensing, actuation, tunability, and wave control.
Contents:
Introduction [2 lectures]: Introduction to smart materials and smart structures, Classification of smart materials,
Applications in sensing, actuation, and energy harvesting.
Review of Non-linear Mechanics [7 Lectures]: Kinematics: Configurations and motion of continuum bodies,
deformation gradient, strain tensors; Stress and the balance principles: conservation of mass, the momentum
principles, the Cauchy stress tensor, stress measures for large deformations, the equations of motion and symmetry of
stress, balance of mechanical energy, the principles of virtual work and power.
Piezoelectric Materials [6 Lectures]: History of Piezoelectricity, Piezoelectric Materials, Direct and converse
piezoelectric effects; constitutive behaviour and governing equations; electromechanical coupling coefficients and
energy conversion, modeling and engineering applications.
Electroactive Polymers and Soft Actuation [6 Lectures]: Electro-active polymers and their classification,
electrostatic actuation mechanisms, Dielectric elastomers, nonlinear electromechanical coupling and governing
equations, large deformation response; electro-mechanical instabilities and pull-in phenomena; modeling and
engineering applications.
Magneto-Active Materials [6 Lectures]: Magnetostriction; hard and soft magneto-active elastomers,
magnetorheological elastomers; magneto-mechanical constitutive behavior; magnetic body forces and Maxwell stress;
magneto-mechanical instabilities, modeling and engineering applications.
Architected Materials and Structures [6 Lectures]: Homogenization and effective properties of heterogeneous
media; lattice and cellular structures; auxetic response and negative Poisson’s ratio; architected stiffness and damping;
structural instabilities as design tools; metastructures with embedded smart materials for tunable response.
Wave Control and Tunable Phononic Structures [6 Lectures]: Wave propagation in periodic media; dispersion
relations; Bragg scattering and bandgap formation; locally resonant structural systems; vibration attenuation and
isolation; active and tunable phononic structures using smart materials.

Course_Title:
Objectives:
1.​ The objective of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles,
technologies, and methodologies of Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) for engineering structures.
2.​ The course aims to develop a strong foundation in SHM philosophy, sensing mechanisms, data acquisition,
and decision-making frameworks, with an emphasis on smart materials, including piezoelectric,
magnetostrictive, and optical fiber sensors.
Learning Outcomes: The student will have ability to
1. Analyze local vibration and impedance-based SHM data using piezoelectric and smart material-based sensing
techniques.
2. Select appropriate sensors, install SHM systems on real structures, and evaluate sensor performance and
diagnostics.
3. Apply global vibration techniques to extract modal parameters such as natural frequencies and mode shapes for
damage detection.
Contents-
Introduction to SHM [10 Lectures]: An overview of Structural Health Monitoring: definition, objectives, and
philosophy. SHM framework: sensing, data acquisition, feature extraction, and decision making. SHM versus
Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE): similarities and differences. Levels of damage identification: detection,
localization, quantification, prognosis. Overview of sensor systems and performance requirements for SHM. Smart
materials for SHM: definition and classification. Piezoelectric materials: basic physics, constitutive relations, sensing
and actuation. Magnetostrictive materials: fundamentals, magnetization and hysteresis behaviour. Optical fiber
sensors and Lamb wave–based SHM methods. Emerging SHM technologies using piezo, magnetostrictive, and
optical fiber sensors. Solution domain for SHM and commonly used damage indices. Overview of application
potential of SHM in mechanical, aerospace, civil infrastructures, and other engineering systems.
Sensing and Data Acquisition System [10 Lectures]: Strain gauges, displacement sensors, accelerometers. Fiber
Bragg Grating (FBG) sensors and optical sensing principles. Acoustic emission sensors and piezoelectric transducers.
Embedded and surface-mounted sensors for composites, metals, and concrete. Wireless sensor networks, energy
harvesting sensors, and sensor placement optimization. Data acquisition hardware/software and sampling
requirements.
Structural Health Monitoring with Piezoelectric and Magnetostrictive Sensors [11 Lectures]: Sensor
technology, Available industrial acousto-ultrasonic systems with piezoelectric sensors, Electro-Mechanical Impedance
(EMI) technique, Delamination Sensing using Piezo Sensory Layer. Voltage response from Piezopatch. SHM using
Magnetostrictive sensory layer. Basics of Magnetization and Hysteresis. Delamination sensing using Magnetostrictive
sensory layer. Constitutive equation for the composite. Magnetostrictive sensory layer in symmetric laminate.
Structural Health Monitoring using Laser Doppler Velocimeter (LDV) or Vibrometer [8 Lectures]: Introduction
to LDV. Experimental Modal Analysis using LDV. Linking experimental and analytical vibration data. Modal
Assurance Criterion (MAC) for mode pairing. Velocity and Displacement Measurement using LDV. Mathematical
description of structural system with damage. Damage localization and quantification. Case study for Symmetric and
Cross-ply laminates.
Text Books:
1.​ Soh, C.K., Yang, Y. and Bhalla, S. eds., 2012. Smart materials in structural health monitoring, control and
biomechanics. Springer Science & Business Media.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
1.​ Provide a fundamental understanding of linear algebra.
2.​ Provide a fundamental understanding of ordinary differential equations.

independence, Basis, Dimensions, Coordinate with respect to a basis, Complementary subspaces, Linear
transformations, Range space and rank, Null space and nullity, Matrix representation of linear transformation,

and eigenvectors, Characteristic polynomials, Cayley-Hamilton theorem, Properties of eigenvalues and
eigenvectors, Diagonalization.

variables, Exact equations, Integrating factors, Solution of IVP, Existence and uniqueness, Picard's theorem for

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
1. Demonstrate the validity and error in the numerical results
2. Explain numerical techniques for a variety of problems
3. Introduce how to solve numerically algebraic equations, linear systems of equations, approximation and ordinary
differential equations.

The students will have the ability to:
1. Develop an understanding of numerical error and applicability of a particular method.
2. Solve numerically algebraic equations, linear systems of equations and ordinary differential equations.

Errors in computation [Lecture 2]: Numerical Algorithms and errors, source and types of errors, error propagation, floating
point representation, rounding error and floating point arithmetic.

schemes (LU, QR, spectral, Schur, polar, SVD).

Newton-Cotes formulas, Gauss quadrature rules, and Method of Undetermined Coefficients.

methods, Runge-Kutta Methods, adaptive methods, BVP finite difference methods, introduction to parallel computation.

reaction mechanisms.
2. To broaden their understanding of organic chemistry with emphasis on the efficiency
and selectivity of organic reactions.

The students are expected to:
1. Be able to propose mechanisms for complex organic reactions.

a a b a

diastereoselectivity, stereoselectivity, and stereospecificity in organic reactions; chiral pool
synthesis (8 lectures).

halogenation of alkanes; Named reactions involving radical intermediates (5 lectures).

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
1. Provide the connection between microscopic theory and thermodynamics.
2. Describe how complex phenomena can be transferred into simple models.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to:
1. Predict properties of many-body systems starting from its microscopic constituents
and their interactions
2. Connect microscopic theory to chemical reaction
Contents
Mathematical foundation: Probability theory, Permutation and combination, Conditional
probability and independent events, Random variables and their probability distribution,
Central limit theorem, Binomial distribution, Stirling’s approximation, Method of Lagrange
multiplier; Statistics of scientific measurement, Error, Maximum likelihood method, Curve
fitting, Least square fit; Dirac delta function, Uniform distribution and Dirac delta function,
Partial differential equation, equation of continuity (11 Lectures)
Statistical thermodynamics: Micro and Macro states, postulates, concepts of distinguishable
and indistinguishable particles, Microcanonical Ensemble (NVE), Canonical Ensembles or
Isothermal-isochoric (NVT) Ensembles, Isothermal-isobaric (NPT) and Grand Canonical
Ensemble (μVT), Equivalence of Ensembles, Boltzmann distribution, Entropy, partition
functions for different ensemble, calculations of thermodynamic properties of each of
ensemble, ideal monatomic and diatomic gas, Applications of canonical ensemble, 1D Ising
model, Ideal and real gas, Sackur Tetrode equation, Phase space, Ergodicity, Liouville’s
Theorem (15 Lectures)
Applications: Fluctuations and thermodynamic properties, Heat capacity, compressibility,
Linear response theory, Partition function and Transition State Theory, classical fluids, Pair
correlation functions, Response functions, Langevin Equation, Fluctuation-Dissipation
Theorem, Diffusion (13 Lectures)

and material properties.
2. Provide an interdisciplinary understanding of solid state chemistry which aims to
provide an understanding of how molecular structure affects the properties of
materials.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
1. Introduce a few spectroscopic methods used as analytical techniques in various
fields of science and engineering.
2. Provide conceptual background of these methods along with their instrumentation
and some applications.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Understand the conceptual background of various spectroscopic techniques
2. Connect quantum mechanics and spectroscopy to interpret experimental findings
in research.
Contents
Fundamentals: Electromagnetic radiation, Maxwell’s equations, Time-dependent
perturbation theory, Interaction of radiation with matter, Intensity of a Transition -
Transition Dipole Moment, Fermi’s golden rule; Einstein treatment, Lasers and line shapes
and line broadening, Laser spectroscopy; Spectroscopic Timescales, Selection rule for
photon-molecule interaction, Continuous wave and Fourier Transform spectroscopy,
Sensitivity and resolution of spectrum, Instrumentation, Dispersive spectrometers, Fourier
Transform spectrometers (10 Lectures)
Rotational Spectroscopy: Linear Motion and Rotational Motion, Diatomic Rigid Rotor,
Derivation of selection rules for microwave spectra, Isotope effect, Degeneracy, Intensity of
Rotational Lines, Non-Rigid Rotor, Polyatomic Molecules, Rotational Raman Spectroscopy
(5 Lectures)
Vibrational Spectroscopy: Simple harmonic oscillator, Selection rules, Anharmonicity and its
effects, Rotational-vibrational spectra, Normal modes of Vibration, FT-IR Spectroscopy,
Vibrational Raman spectroscopy (7 Lectures)
Electronic spectroscopy: Basic principle, Symmetry and Term Symbols, Born-Oppenheimer
approximation, vibrational coarse and rotational fine structures, Vibrational Progression,
Pre-dissociation, Selection rules from transition moment integral – Spin selection, Laporte
selection, Frank-Condon principle. Jablonski diagram, various photophysical processes,
quantum yield expression, Chromophores, Types of electronic transition, Effect of
conjugation and solvent. Introduction to photoelectron spectroscopy. (8 Lectures)
Magnetic resonance Spectroscopy: Origin of spin and magnetic moment, Zeeman splitting and
gyromagnetic ratio, Electron and nuclear spin resonance, Instrumentation, NMR chemical
shift and spin-spin coupling, introduction to AB, AX, AMX spin system, 1D 1H and 13 NMR
experiments, Pulse sequences; Methods of relaxation, Double resonance techniques; EPR –
Instrumentation, First Derivative Spectra, Electron-nuclear hyperfine interaction, theory of
first order EPR spectra, analysis of 1st Order spectra, example of EPR spectra of organic
radicals and transition metal complexes. (9 Lectures)
Textbook
1. Banwell, C. N., (1994), Fundamentals of Molecular Spectroscopy, 3rd Edition, Tata
McGraw-Hill
2. Book Company.
3. Bernath, P. F., (2005), Spectra of Atoms and Molecules, 2nd Edition, Oxford
University Press
4. J. M. Hollas, Modern Spectroscopy, Wiley India Exclusive, 2015

Course_Title:
Objective
The instructor will guide to:
1. Understand the fundamental principles of stereoselective and asymmetric synthesis/catalysis.
2. Explore various strategies and methods in asymmetric catalysis, biocatalysis, organo-catalysis,
transition metal catalysis and dual catalysis.
3. Appreciate the applications of asymmetric synthesis in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and
industrially relevant molecules.
Learning Outcomes
Students will be able to:
1. Grasp the key principles and strategies behind asymmetric catalysis and synthesis.
2. Understand and apply different methods, biocatalysis, organocatalytic and transition metal-
catalysed reactions.
3. Analyse and evaluate how asymmetric synthesis is used to create important molecules in
pharmaceuticals, industry, and biology.
Contents
Principles of Selectivity: Chemoselectivity, regioselectivity, stereoselectivity, and stereospecificity. (4
Lectures), importance of chirality. Basics of asymmetric catalysis, including energetics of reactions.
Asymmetric Resolution: Kinetic resolution (KR), parallel kinetic resolution (PKR), dynamic kinetic
resolution (DKR), dynamic kinetic asymmetric transformation (DyKAT), desymmetrization (DS). (5
Lectures)
Asymmetric Biocatalysis: It includes the principles of enzyme catalysis, stereoselective reactions such as
enzymatic oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis, and their applications (5 Lectures)
Asymmetric Metal Catalysis: The study of using transition-metal catalysts such as Rh, Ru, Pd, Ir, Ni, Co
and Cu and chiral Lewis’s acid catalysis. Enantioselective reduction and oxidation; Sharpless
asymmetric epoxidation (8 Lectures)
Asymmetric Organocatalysis: Fundamentals of organocatalysts, including thiourea-based catalysts, N-
heterocyclic carbenes, hydrogen-bonding catalysts, Brønsted acid and base catalysis, and phase-transfer
catalysts. (8 Lectures)
Metal-Organo Dual Catalysis: Cooperative mechanisms, enamine, iminium, counterion, N-heterocyclic
carbenes. (5 Lectures)
Applications of Asymmetric Catalysis: Pharmaceuticals (e.g., Thalidomide, L-DOPA), agrochemicals (e.g.,
Metolachlor), and industrial chiral molecules (e.g., flavors, fragrances). (4 Lectures)
Text Books
1. I. Ojima., (2010), Catalytic Asymmetric Synthesis, John Wiley & Sons, New Jersey, 3rd Ed.
2. E. N. Jacobsen, A. Pfaltz, H. Yamamoto., (1999), Comprehensive Asymmetric Catalysis III,
Springer-Verlag, Berlin Heidelberg, Germany.
3. P. J. Walsh, M. C. Kozlowski., (2009), Fundamentals of Asymmetric Catalysis, University Science
Books, USA.
4. R. E. Gawley, J. Aube., (2002), Principles of Asymmetric Synthesis, Springer, New York.
References Books
1. B. A. Arndtsen, L.-Z. Gong., (2020), Asymmetric Organocatalysis Combined with Metal Catalysis,
Springer, Berlin.
