Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will:
1. Introduce students to structures and functions of organic biomolecules.
2. Impart comprehensive knowledge on chemical synthesis can be applied to
engineer new biomolecules for modern applications.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
1. Describe the structures, chemical properties, and functions of biomolecules.
2. Integrate fundamental concepts to conceptualize and design chemical technology
for bio-applications.
Course Contents
Introduction: Organic chemistry of living systems, pH and buffers, Covalent and non-
covalent interactions in organic and biological world, Analogy between organic chemistry
and biochemical reactions (3 Lectures)
Chemistry of Amino Acids: Structure and properties of amino acids, amide-coupling
reactions, amine/acid protection and deprotection protocols, Ninhydrin test for amino
acids, Synthesis of non-canonical and unnatural amino acids and applications, Peptides
and solid-state peptide synthesis, Protein secondary structure, Characterization of
peptides and proteins using NMR, mass, etc. (8 lectures)
Chemistry of Enzymes: Classification and properties of enzymes, thermodynamics and
kinetics of enzyme catalysis, catalytic mechanisms, enzyme inhibition and drug design,
Industrial application of a few enzymes: in organic transformation and fermentation;
enzyme as medicine/drug; Abzymes in organic transformation such as Diels Alder,
Baldwin’s rule, Oxy-Cope rearrangement (6 lectures)
Chemistry of Nucleic Acids: Sugars and organic bases; Nomenclature, Conformation of
sugar-phosphate backbone, Nucleotide chemistry and tautomerism, Hydrogen bonding
by bases, -stacking interactions and DNA intercalators, Chemical synthesis and
application of unnatural nucleosides in modern technologies (7 lectures)
Chemistry of carbohydrates and fatty acids: Carbohydrates: stereochemistry, Haworth and
chair notations, epimers and anomers, mutarotation, glycosidic bonds, chemical synthesis
and degradation of monosaccharides, nitrogen containing sugars, applications in drug
delivery systems. Structure and types of lipids, chemical synthesis of artificial lipids for
modern applications. (10 lectures)
Chemistry of terpenes, terpenoids and steroids: Classification, chemical structures, systematic
nomenclature, Isoprene rule, Biosynthesis of terpenes and cyclization mechanisms and
origin of non-classical carbocation rearrangement, cholesterol and its role; Biosynthesis;
application of terpenes, such as Eucalyptus oil, Isolation techniques for industrial
applications (5 lectures)
Textbooks
1. T. W. Graham Solomons, C. B. Fryhle, S. A. Snyder. Organic Chemistry. 12th
Edition, Wiley.
2. D. V. Vranken and G. A. Weiss. Introduction to Bioorganic Chemistry and Chemical
Biology. Garland Science; 1st edition, 2012

Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will:
Provide an introduction to various characterization methods that are applied to inorganic chemical
systems.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to:
1. Explore different important characterization methods that are applied to inorganic chemical
systems.
2. Analyse the chemical and physical characterization of molecular (solution and solid- state)
inorganic chemical systems.
Contents
Fundamental aspects of characterization methods in inorganic chemistry.
Molecular Symmetry: Point group analysis of simple inorganic compounds. Infrared and Raman
spectroscopy of simple inorganic molecules; predicting number of active modes of vibrations, analysis

Electronic spectroscopy: Electronic absorption and emission spectroscopy (4 Lectures)

Lectures)
EPR: Elementary aspects of Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy of inorganic
compounds- g-values, hyperfine and super hyperfine coupling constants; selected applications in
inorganic chemistry. (5 Lectures)
Mass spectrometry: basic principles, ionization techniques, isotope abundance, molecular ion;
illustrative examples from supramolecules, inorganic/coordination and organometallic compounds.
(5 Lectures)
X-Ray and Photoelectron Spectroscopy: Electron microscopy and energy dispersive analysis of X-rays (5
Lectures)
Cyclic voltammetry: Introduction to cyclic voltammetry and discussion on cyclic voltammogram of
some representative examples. (3 Lectures)

Course_Title:

1. Give better insights into the interesting class of compounds such as rings, clusters, polymers
and low valent complexes of the main-group elements.
2. Provide learning about the synthesis, structure and properties of inorganic heterocyclic and
homocyclic rings.
3. Discuss structure, properties and reactivity of clusters and cages of main group elements.

The students are expected to:

polyphosphazenes, polysilanes and organometallic polymers. (10 Lectures)

Course_Title:
Objectives
1.​ This course examines how knowledge and research are generated and
used in the field of social sciences.
2.​ To understand major issues in epistemology and the philosophy of science
concerning what we can know about the world, including a discussion of
discipline-based and interdisciplinary approaches.
3.​ Explores basic principles of research theory, with attention to the advantages
and disadvantages of research designs such as aggregate analysis, small-n
comparisons, and case studies.
4.​ To appreciate the role of computational methods in social sciences.
Learning Outcomes
1.​ To understand how knowledge and research are generated and used in the field of
social sciences.
2.​ Learn about major issues in epistemology and the philosophy of science concerning
what we can know about the world, including a discussion of discipline-based and
interdisciplinary approaches.
3.​ Understand different methods of social inquiry.
4.​ To understand the role of computational methods in the social sciences.
Contents
Introduction to epistemology: Theories of knowledge and the role of disciplinary
approaches to it; history and philosophy of science; advantages and disadvantages of
interdisciplinary approaches; ambiguities of knowledge generation and the
uncertainties that surround attempts to know what we know and better (6 lectures)
Philosophy of science and the aims of social science: Nature of knowledge, theory,
and evidence in social Investigation; key steps in ‘science’ progression; claims about the
nature of the world that social scientists make; nature and scope of major social science
disciplines; Hierarchy of Science, Social Science Challenges (6 lectures).
Developing and testing theories: Role of theory generation and theory testing in social
research; diffusion theory, agenda-setting theory, and institutional political economy
versus interest group theory. (7 lectures)
Marrying computational methods with social science: History of CSS; common
grounds between computational methods and social science; fourth paradigm: A 21st
century science; digital revolution. (7 lectures)
Role of computational methods in social sciences: Computational methods in social
science; regression methods for establishing causal relations and their limitations;
computational methods in social policies; secondary datasets and their relevance in
social science research; history, essence and future of agent-based modelling; computer
simulation in solving mysteries of social emergence (11 lectures).
Evolution of CSS field: Difference between computational social science and
conventional social science; emergence of new computational tools and methods;
opportunities and challenges in CSS (2 lectures).
Textbook
●​ Kuhn, Thomas. 1970. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. Chicago: University of
Chicago Press, 2nd edition. ISBN: 0226458121.

Objectives:
●​ To help students conceptualise science and technology as embedded in culture,
politics and society, and understand how technical knowledge is produced in society.
●​ To help students explore the dynamic relationship between technology and society

Course_Title:
Objectives:
●​ The economic growth and development trajectory is vulnerable to business
cycles, which, according to mainstream economics, requires government intervention
from time to time. These interventions are more large-scale when faced with bigger
events such as recessions and financial crises. Why these vulnerabilities exist and why
and these events occur, will be explored, along with the forms that corrective
interventions.
●​ The currently dominant economic system has led to vulnerabilities and
challenges such as obstacles to structural transformation, unemployment, inequality,
poverty, high levels of informality in the economy. Why this is the case and what
policies (if at all) may address these challenges will be explored.
●​ The fourth industrial revolution, characterised by increasing automation and ICT,
presents challenges for production structures and capital-labour relations, and
innovations such as Cryptocurrency, as a decentralised medium of payment, have both
potential and risks in terms of evasion of a central monetary authority whose job is to
stabilise the economy.
●​ All the above larger set of challenges has attracted the attention of empirical
research by economists, which uses Econometric methods as well as economic policy
research, such as impact evaluations using Randomised Controlled Trials. The basic
rationale of these approaches and some of the research findings will be introduced.
Learning Outcomes:
●​ Contextualise mathematical and computational models in contemporary
economic challenges (some of which have lessons learned or unlearnt from the past),
which themselves can be contextualised in a spectrum of macroeconomic as well as
microeconomic schools of thought, in both of which the spectral units are often in
opposition to each other.
●​ Be equipped with a critical thinking outlook and the knowledge foundation, based
on which creative econometric models can be built to address real-world challenges

algebra, differential equations) and their application in modeling and solving complex physical and engineering
systems using ordinary and partial differential equations.
2.​ Introduce foundational concepts in probability and statistics to enable students to interpret data and analyze
uncertainty in engineering processes.
Learning Outcomes
1.​ Students will proficiently apply vector calculus, tensor analysis, matrix operations, and both analytical and
numerical methods for solving ODEs and PDEs to address engineering problems involving multivariable
systems, transformations, and physical contexts like vibrations and heat transfer.
2.​ Students will effectively use statistical methods to analyze experimental data, conduct hypothesis testing, and
develop simple predictive models for engineering applications.

1.​ Vectors & Tensors - Vector Algebra; Functions of several variables; Curves and surfaces; Multiple integrals;

basis & dimension; Orthogonality, projection and least square approximation; Basis Vectors; Determinant
properties; condition number; Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors - including examples; Singular Value
decomposition. [8 lectures]

solutions of ODEs; Laplace transforms; Fourier series; Sturm-Liouville problems; Fourier transforms;

ODE using system of ODEs, stiff problems, Boundary value problem using shooting method.​ ​

string vibrations - Eigen modes etc, Cauchy equilibrium equation-applied on thin elastic plate.​ ​
[4 Lectures]

distributions, distributions of several random variables, random sampling, point estimation, confidence

Course_Title:
Objective:
The Instructor will
1.​ Introduce the fundamental materials and electrochemical principles underlying modern
battery cells, covering electrode and electrolyte materials, interfacial phenomena.
2.​ Explain degradation mechanisms that govern battery performance, energy density, and
lifetime.
Learning Outcomes:
3.​ Identify and compare cathode, anode, and electrolyte materials for various battery
chemistries.
4.​ Explain electrochemical working principles of Li-ion and beyond-Li battery systems.
Contents:
Fundamentals of Electrochemical Energy Storage Thermodynamics of electrochemical cells;
electrode potential and Nernst equation; Faradaic and non-Faradaic processes; cell voltage,
capacity, energy density and power density; Butler-Volmer equation for electrochemical
kinetics; overpotentials and their origins.
Anode Materials: Graphite structure and lithiation mechanism; silicon and tin-based alloy
anodes; lithium titanate (LTO) anodes; lithium metal anodes and dendrite challenges; sodium
and multivalent metal anodes; conversion-type anode materials.
Cathode Materials: Layered oxide cathodes: LCO, NMC, NCA; spinel cathodes: LMO; olivine
cathodes: LFP; high-nickel cathode chemistry; sodium-ion cathodes: layered oxides, Prussian
blue analogues; structural stability and capacity degradation; high-voltage cathode materials.
Electrolyte Materials: Liquid electrolytes: solvents and lithium salts; ionic conductivity and
electrochemical stability window; solid polymer electrolytes; inorganic solid electrolytes: oxide
and sulfide types; Solid Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) formation and stability; electrolyte
additives and their functions.
Separators, Current Collectors, and Cell Architecture: Separator materials and properties;
ceramic-coated separators; current collector materials and surface treatments; cell formats:
cylindrical, pouch, prismatic; pack architecture and design considerations.
Degradation and Failure Mechanisms: Capacity fade mechanisms in Li-ion batteries; lithium
plating and stripping phenomena; mechanical degradation: cracking and delamination;
thermal aging and electrolyte decomposition; calendar and cycle aging models; failure
analysis techniques.

Course_Title:
Objective:
The instructor will provide an insight into:
1.​ Quantitative and computational description of electrochemical processes relevant to
batteries (kinetics, transport, impedance, multiscale modelling).
2.​ Physics-based modelling and numerical simulation of battery cells and packs
(equivalent-circuit and porous-electrode models), AI-driven (machine-learning and
deep-learning) methods for battery state estimation, lifetime prediction, and
diagnostics at the cell and system level.
Learning Outcomes:
The students are expected to have the ability to
3.​ Formulate and solve basic electrochemical models (diffusion, charge transfer,
impedance) numerically for battery-relevant systems.
4.​ Develop and use equivalent-circuit and physics-based models (SPM, P2D) for cell
performance and degradation analysis, Design data pipelines and apply ML/AI
techniques for SOC/SOH estimation, prognostics, and AI-assisted battery design.
Contents:
Computational Electrochemistry Foundations: Chemical vs electrochemical kinetics;
Butler-Volmer equation, Tafel behaviour; transport in electrolytes and electrodes (diffusion,
migration), 1D model set-up; numerical solution of diffusion/kinetics boundary-value
problems; introduction to voltammetry and impedance modelling (Randles circuit, Warburg).
Multiscale and DFT Perspectives for Batteries: Motivation for electronic-structure methods in
batteries; conceptual introduction; typical DFT workflows and outputs; linking DFT-derived
parameters to continuum battery models and databases.
Battery Modelling and Simulation: Brief recap of cell operation and definitions (SOC, SOH,
C-rate) from a modelling perspective; equivalent-circuit models; parameter identification
from pulse/HPPC tests; porous-electrode theory, single-particle model and pseudo-2D
models; numerical solution strategies (discretization, time stepping, stiffness); simple
degradation modeling (SEI growth, resistance increase) and validation against data.
AI-Driven Battery Design & Diagnostics: Overview of AI/ML for batteries (supervised
learning, deep learning, physics-informed models); data sources and pipelines for cell and
pack data; feature engineering from cycling and field datasets; SOC/SOH estimation with
classical filters and ML regressors; deep time-series models (RNN/CNN/LSTM) and
physics-informed neural networks as surrogates for battery models; AI-assisted design and
lifetime prediction workflows.

Course_Title:
Objectives:
1. To orient students towards usage of data driven approaches and machine learning algorithms for solving problems
in the field composite materials.
2. To train students with hands-on learning experiences on various case studies involving prediction, classification
and generative modeling of composite materials design and properties.
Learning outcomes:
1. Ability to apply modern AI/ML tools in analyzing and solving problems related to composite materials.
2. Ability in handling, analysis, interpretation and generation of big data in composite materials domain.
Course Content
Module 1: Big Data in Composite Materials (6 Lectures)
Dataset creation from experiments, simulations, and literature data mining; statistical analysis; correlations, handling
missing data, dataset imbalances, dimensionality reduction and visualization of high-dimensional datasets, feature
generation and elimination techniques, data leakage in machine learning workflows, data distributions during training and
inference, and efficient data loading techniques for large datasets. Hands on training session on programming in python,
data types, functions, loops, and importing python libraries, Data handling, visualization, heatmaps, correlations in
datasets.

Supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and generative learning paradigms, bias and variance trade-off, underfitting and
overfitting, classification, regression and clustering problems, linear and logistic regression, ridge and lasso regression, code
demonstration on application of supervised learning in damage mode identification of composites. Implementing linear
models for composite materials through scikit learn, effect of regularization.

such as bagging and boosting; model interpretation techniques including feature importance analysis, code demonstration
on application of regression models in physical property prediction of polymer composites. Bayesian optimization,
surrogate modeling and inverse materials design.

Architecture of artificial neural networks, activation functions, training using backpropagation, and optimization
algorithms. Model explanation by SHAP and LIME, Fatigue life prediction of polymer composites using ANN
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) including convolution operations and pooling; advanced architectures such as U-Net

Poisson’ ratio, demonstration of defects detection using U-Net/ResNet.

Course_Title:
Objective:
1.​ To introduce the fundamental concepts of stress, strain, and constitutive relations in
elastic solids and develop the mathematical framework required to analyze
deformation and stress distribution in engineering materials and structures.
2.​ The course aims to provide analytical tools for solving boundary value problems in
elasticity and to understand classical solutions involving torsion, bending, and energy
methods.
Learning Outcomes:
1.​ Apply the concepts of stress, strain, and constitutive relations to analyze deformation
and stress distribution in elastic solids. Determine principal stresses, shear stresses,
and material response under different loading conditions.
2.​ Formulate and solve basic boundary value problems in linear elasticity and analyze
torsion and bending of structural members. Apply energy principles and approximate
methods to estimate stresses and deflections in engineering structures.
Contents:
Stress and Equilibrium [6 Lectures]: Cartesian tensors, Index notation, Internal forces
and equilibrium, Traction vector and Cauchy’s theorem, Stress tensor and its properties,
Transformation of stress components, Normal and shear stresses, Principal stresses and
principal directions, Maximum shear stress, Linear and angular momentum balance,
Mohr’s circle, Stress invariants, Decomposition of stress tensor, Octahedral stresses.
Kinematics of deformation and Strain [6 Lectures]: Local state of deformation at a
material point, Displacement gradients and deformation tensor, Green-Lagrange Strain
Tensor, Euler-Almansi Strain Tensor, Small strain tensor, Physical interpretation of strain
components, Transformation of strain components, Strain invariants, Compatibility of
strains.
Constitutive Equations and Material Failure [7 Lectures]: Linear elasticity and
Hooke's Law, Elasticity tensor and transformation of basis, Symmetries of the stiffness
tensor, Engineering or Voigt notation, Material symmetries and anisotropy, Isotropic linear
elastic materials, Elastic constants (Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, shear modulus, bulk
modulus), Thermoelastic effects, Particular states of stress and strain of interest: Uniaxial
stress, Uniaxial strain, Plane stress, Plane strain, Failure criteria: Maximum normal stress,
Tresca Yield Criterion, Von Mises Yield Criterion, Octahedral shear stress, Distortion strain
energy theory.
Boundary value problems in linear elasticity [7 Lectures]: Summary of field
equations, Displacement formulation, Navier's Equations, Stress formulation,
Beltrami-Michell Equations, Principle of superposition, Saint-Venant's Principle,
Two-dimensional problems in elasticity, Plane stress problems, Plane strain problems, Airy
Stress Function.
Torsion [5 Lectures]: Formulation of the basic equations of torsion of prismatic bars,
Prandtl Stress Function, Torsion of noncircular bars, Warping function formulation,
Membrane analogy, Torsion of bars with hollow thick-wall sections, Torsion of bars with
thin hollow cross-sections.
Bending of Beams [4 Lectures]: Simple beam theory, Stress and strain distribution in
pure bending, Generalization of simple beam theory to three dimensions and general
cross sections, Combined effects of bending, shear, and torsion.

Course_Title:
Objective: The objective is to
1.​ Develop a rigorous understanding of the finite element method (FEM) and its
application to the numerical solution of differential equations arising in engineering
problems.
2.​ Formulate, implement, and interpret results for scalar- and vector-valued problems,
including time-dependent and eigenvalue analyses.
Learning Outcomes: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
1.​ Derive finite element formulations using direct and variational approaches.
2.​ Implement finite element formulations for bars, beams, heat transfer, and elasticity
problems.
Contents
Introduction [4 Lectures]: Background; roadmap in FE-analysis, applications of finite
elements; Direct approach for discrete systems: bar element, equation for assembly,
boundary conditions, and system solution, applications to other linear systems,
transformation laws, truss systems.
Variational approaches [5 Lectures]: Functional, variational operator, Euler-Lagrange
equation, governing differential equations, and associated functional form. Rayleigh-Ritz
Method, weighted residual approach, collocation method, least square method, Galerkin
approach, weak formulation. Trial function, Test function.
Finite element formulation for 1D problems [4 Lectures]: FEM approach, Local
approximation function and global approximation function, convergence, continuity, and
completeness. Compatibility. Weak form for bar with varying cross-section, 1D linear
shape function, Discrete equation, Local and global stiffness matrix, force vector from
weak form. Numerical integration, Gauss quadrature, Transformation from physical space
to parent space.
FE-formulation for Beam elements [4 Lectures]: Beam theory, governing differential
equation and boundary conditions, Weak formulation, Hermite shape function, Derivation
of local stiffness matrix, Force vector, numerical examples with beam and bar element.
FE-formulation for two-dimensional scalar-valued problems [4 Lectures]:
Two-dimensional scalar-valued problem. Governing differential equation of the heat
conduction with boundary conditions. Weak formulation, Approximation function, Pascal’s
triangle, Triangular element shape function derivation, FE-formulation of heat equation.
Rectangular element shape function.
Isoparametric element and numerical integration [3 Lectures]: Isoparametric
element. Shape function for a quadrilateral element. Transformation: physical space to
parent space. Gauss quadrature in two dimensions. Compatibility and hanging nodes
issue. Triangular element. Gauss quadrature points and weights for a triangular domain.
FE-formulation for two-dimensional vector-valued problems [4 Lectures]:
Two-dimensional vector-valued problem. Governing differential equation elasticity
equation. Plane stress and plane strain. Weak formulation, FE-formulation.

Background [3 Lectures]: Historical development, Review of crack-tip fields in linear
elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM); Modes of fracture (I, II, III), Analytical solution of
plane crack problems, stress intensity factors, energy release rate, and their equivalence.

Critical energy release rate; R-curve behavior and fracture stability, concept of J-integral
(path independence), Relation between G and J, Introduction to elastic-plastic fracture

Method for determining fracture parameters, Domain and interaction integral approach.

diffuse approaches, Phase-field model for fracture, derivation of governing equations from
variational principle, Length-scale parameter and regularization; Phase-field for brittle
fracture (AT model, phase-field evolution); Extensions to fatigue; Advantages over
discrete methods (no explicit crack tracking, natural branching/coalescence); Numerical

Course_Title:
Objectives
1.​ To introduce the fundamental principles governing the dynamics of mechanical
systems subjected to time-varying loads.
2.​ To develop the ability to formulate and analyze equations of motion for discrete
and continuous mechanical systems using classical and variational methods.
Learning Outcomes: Students will be able to
1.​ Formulate equations of motion for mechanical systems using Newtonian and
2.​ energy-based approaches and analyze their dynamic behavior.
Contents:
Introduction [2 Lectures]: Overview and objectives of dynamics of mechanical
systems. Types of dynamic loading. Essential characteristics of dynamic problems.
Classification of mechanical systems: discrete and continuous systems. Distinction
between rigid body dynamics and vibration analysis. Engineering applications of system
dynamics.
Preliminaries of rigid body dynamics [6 Lectures]: Rigid body description and
coordinate systems. Position and orientation representation. Rotation matrices and their
properties. Homogeneous transformation matrices and coordinate transformations. Linear
and angular velocity of a rigid body. Skew-symmetric angular velocity matrix. Space-fixed
and body-fixed angular velocity descriptions. Linear and angular acceleration. Coriolis and
centripetal acceleration. Mass distribution and inertia of rigid bodies. Properties of the
inertia matrix and principal moments of inertia.
Formulations for system dynamics [6 Lectures]: Formulation of equations of motion
for mechanical systems. Newton’s laws and D’Alembert’s principle. Generalized
coordinates and generalized forces. Lagrange’s equations of motion. Energy methods and
functionals. Variational formulations in mechanics. Hamilton’s principle and its application
to mechanical system dynamics.
Dynamics of discrete systems [13 Lectures]: Single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF)
system dynamics. Free vibration and forced vibration analysis. Response to harmonic,
periodic, and impulsive excitations. Duhamel’s convolution integral for dynamic response.
Vibration isolation and transmissibility. Response to general dynamic loading. Fourier
series representation of periodic loading. Multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) systems:
formulation of equations of motion. Matrix representation of mass, damping, and
stiffness. Modal analysis and modal superposition techniques.
Dynamics of continuous systems [12 Lectures]: Introduction to distributed
parameter systems. Governing equations and boundary conditions. Free and forced
vibration of strings. Longitudinal vibration of bars. Transverse vibration of beams.
Torsional vibration of shafts. Analytical solution techniques for continuous systems.
Approximate methods: Rayleigh’s method and Rayleigh-Ritz method for estimating natural
frequencies and mode shapes.

Objective:
1.​ To introduce the nonlinear mechanics of soft materials such as rubbers, gels, and
biological tissues, focusing on large deformations and nonlinear constitutive behavior.
2.​ The course develops the continuum mechanics and energy-based modeling framework
needed to analyze instabilities, soft actuators, and failure in soft material systems.

1.​ Understand and apply nonlinear continuum mechanics and constitutive models to
analyze large deformations and material behavior in soft materials.
2.​ Analyze mechanical instabilities, failure mechanisms, and soft actuators using
energy-based and continuum modeling approaches.
Contents:
Introduction [7 Lectures]: Introduction to soft materials: rubber-like materials,
polymer gels, elastomers, and soft biological tissues; characteristic features such as large
deformations, nonlinear stress-strain behavior, and coupled physical responses.
Mathematical preliminaries: physical quantities and their classification; scalars, vectors,
and tensors; index notation; vector operations (dot, cross, and dyadic products);
representation of partial differentiation using comma notation; gradient, divergence, and
curl of tensors and their representation using index notation.
Nonlinear Continuum Mechanics [10 Lectures]: Kinematics of deformation:
configurations and motion of continuum bodies, deformation mapping, deformation
gradient, and strain measures for large deformations. Stress measures and balance laws:
conservation of mass, balance of linear momentum, Cauchy stress tensor, stress
measures for finite deformation, equations of motion, symmetry of stress tensor, balance

materials; objectivity; material symmetry and isotropic hyperelasticity;
stress–deformation relations in terms of invariants; stress–deformation relations in terms

energy density functions: neo-Hookean, Mooney-Rivlin, Ogden, Gent, Fung material, etc.;
anisotropic hyperelastic materials and constitutive modeling.
Viscoelastic Materials [5 Lectures]: Coupling of elasticity and viscosity; kinematics of
viscoelastic deformation; multiplicative decomposition of deformation gradient;
rheological models; internal variable formulation; dissipation inequality and
thermodynamic restrictions; constitutive and evolution equations.
Applications and Instabilities [9 Lectures]: Homogeneous deformation of
hyperelastic membranes under uniaxial and biaxial loading; balloon inflation problem;
energy method for the inflation of a spherical membrane; inflation of arteries under blood
pressure; electroactive membranes; energy method for electroactive membranes;
mechanical instabilities including snap-through instability and the Biot instability;
morphological instabilities such as wrinkles, creases, folds, and ridges.

Course_Title:
Objectives
This course aims to provide advanced understanding of modern power system operation, optimization, and
control. It covers economic dispatch, optimal power flow, load frequency and voltage control, state
estimation, and security assessment. The course also addresses operational challenges arising from
renewable energy integration, uncertainty, and market-based frameworks.
Learning Outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
1.​ Formulate and solve economic dispatch, unit commitment, and optimal power flow problems.
2.​ Analyze load frequency and voltage control in interconnected power systems.
3.​ Apply state estimation and monitoring techniques for reliable system operation.
4.​ Evaluate system security and contingency management strategies.
5.​ Assess the impact of renewable energy and market mechanisms on power system operation.
Contents
Module 1: Economic Operation of Power Systems (8 Hours) Economic dispatch formulation -
Transmission loss modeling and penalty factors - Unit commitment problem formulation - Hydro-thermal
coordination - Classical solution methods - Introduction to security constrained economic dispatch.
Module 2: Optimal Power Flow (8 Hours) DC Optimal Power Flow formulation - AC OPF formulation -
Equality and inequality constraints - Interior point methods overview - Security constrained OPF -
Introduction to convex relaxations.
Module 3: Power System Control (7 Hours) Automatic Generation Control (AGC) - Load frequency control
in single and multi- area systems - Tie-line power control - Governor and turbine models - Excitation
systems and voltage control - Reactive power and voltage control mechanisms.
Module 4: Power System State Estimation and Monitoring (6 Hours) Measurement modeling - Weighted
Least Squares state estimation - Observability analysis - Bad data detection and identification - Phasor
Measurement Units (PMUs) - Introduction to dynamic state estimation.
Module 5: Security and Operational Planning (5 Hours) Security assessment in operational time frame -
Preventive and corrective control actions - Remedial action schemes - Contingency constrained operation -
Introduction to ancillary services.
Module 6: Modern Topics in Power System Operation (5 Hours) Operation with renewable energy sources
- Forecasting and uncertainty in system op- eration - Demand response and distributed energy resource
coordination - Market-based operation and locational marginal pricing - Overview of Energy Management
Systems.

energy storage, carbon capture, refrigeration cycles, and fuel cells, emphasizing chemical equilibrium
and kinetics.

Maxwell relations, Clausius-Clapeyron equation), and Gibbs phase rule to analyze entropy, exergy,

advanced applications (e.g., adiabatic flame temperature, organic Rankine cycles, supercritical CO
2

Course_Title:
Objectives: The course aims to:
1.​ Introduce key principles, models and cognitive foundations of interaction design.
2.​ Develop skills to design, prototype, and evaluate interactive systems grounded in usability,
accessibility, and cognitive principles.
3.​ Prepare students to design for emerging technologies and multimodal systems, with an
awareness of ethical and inclusive practices.
Learning outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1.​ Design and prototype interactive systems that are intuitive, accessible, and user-centered.

and usability metrics.

Foundations of interaction design (5 lectures): Definition, scope, and evolution of interaction
design. Key frameworks: Conceptual models, interaction models and UX layers. Cognitive

constraints and mappings. Visual perception and layout principles, Navigation models.

summative. Methods: Heuristics, cognitive walkthrough, usability testing, A/B testing, analytics.

Advanced interaction paradigms and ethics (4 lectures): Explores emerging interaction modes.
Multimodal interaction: Voice, touch, gesture, gaze, haptics, ambient feedback. Adaptive, XR,
spatial, and conversational interfaces. Human-AI collaboration: Transparency, explainability, trust.

design.

design requirements

feedback for final deliverables

Course_Title:
Objectives: The course aims to:
1.​ Introduce theoretical principles and cognitive foundations of data visualization.
2.​ Enable students to design effective and inclusive visualizations grounded in perception,
interaction design, and storytelling.
3.​ Develop the ability to think critically and creatively about how data can be represented,
interpreted, and communicated through visual design.
Learning outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1.​ Design data visualizations that are clear, usable, and aligned with user needs and data types.
2.​ Assess the effectiveness of data visualizations in supporting understanding, decision-making,
and responsible communication of data.
Contents
Foundations of data visualisation (8 lectures): Definition, scope, and evolution of data
visualisation. Roles and purposes. Types of data: Understanding quantitative, categorical, ordinal,
and temporal data. Data tasks: Comparison, distribution, relationship, and composition. Visual
variables and encoding: Position, length, area, color, shape, and their application in encoding data.

and explanatory visualizations. Perception, hierarchy and cognitive load in data visualization.

Managing visual complexity to enhance readability and comprehension. Structuring and organizing
information to support clarity, hierarchy, and user navigation. Designing multi-level and comparative
views. Integrating visualizations into digital systems. Design strategies for dashboards and
information-dense displays. Designing for responsive and adaptive contexts. Accessibility in data
visualization.
Interactive data storytelling (6 lectures): Role of interaction in data exploration and
comprehension. Interaction techniques: filtering, zooming, panning, etc. Visual storytelling: Framing,
sequencing, and annotation. Narrative structures of data: Temporal, hierarchical, spatial,
comparative, and anecdotal narrative structures. Storytelling for insight, advocacy, decision support.
Evaluation, ethics, and future trends (4 lectures): Evaluation techniques for data visualizations.
Measuring impact. Bias in data and design. Misleading visualizations. Ethical principles in data
representations. Emotional impact and visual rhetoric. Emerging trends in data visualisation.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will:
1. Provide basic understanding of all areas of chemistry: inorganic, organic, and physical.
2. Impart depth of knowledge involving chemical principles to apply concepts in any scientifci
discipline
Learning Outcomes
The student will be able to
1. Describe the concepts involved in major chemical processes
2. Interpret intermediates to solve reactions and mechanisms
Contents
In-organic Chemistry: Introduction to Organometallic Chemistry, 18 electron rule, Common
organometallic ligands and their bonding, Oxidative addition, Reductive elimination, Selective
applications. Introduction to Solid State Chemistry; Types of solids, Symmetry in crystals, Bravais
lattice, unit cell, X-ray diffraction, Braggs law, Structure of crystalline solids such as NaCl, Diamond.
(13 Lectures)
Organic Chemistry: Mechanism and Intermediates: Reaction mechanisms and different methods for
their determination, Isomerization, Resonance, Inductive effect, hyperconjugation, structure and
reactivity of carbocation including nonclassical carbocation, carbanion, radical, carbene, nitrene,
concerted and stepwise mechanism, transition states and intermediates, early and late transition
states, exothermic and endothermic reactions with examples. (13 Lectures)
Physical Chemistry: Probability. Average, Central Limit Theorem, Binomial distribution, Stirling’s
approximation, Microstate, Macrostate, NVT, NVE ensemble, Boltzmann distribution, signifciance of
Boltzmann distribution in physical chemistry, Average vs observed quantity, defni ition of entropy, 2nd
law of thermodynamics, heat capacity, Helmholtz and Gibbs free energy. (13 Lectures)
Laboratory Experiments:
Extraction: Separation of an Acidic, a Basic and a Neutral Substance, Green Chemistry: A Solvent-Free
Aldol Condensation; Solid phase Synthesis and characterization of trans bis glycinato Cu(II); Synthesis
and characterization of acetylferrocene from ferrocene; Determination of equilibrium constant by
partition method, Determination of free energy from equilibrium constant using UV-visible
spectroscopy.
Textbooks
1.​ J.D. Lee, Concise Inorganic Chemistry, (5th Edition), ELBS, 1996.
2.​ R.T. Morrison and R.N. Boyd, Organic Chemistry, Prentice Hall of India Pvt. Ltd., 5th Ed, 1990
3.​ D. A. McQuarrie, Physical Chemistry: A Molecular Approach, Viva Books, 2017.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will:
1.​ Attempt to provide fundamental aspects of theory in view of foundations of quantum chemistry
2.​ Discuss a few applications of quantum theory to chemistry
3.​ Establish the relation between fundamentals of spectroscopy and quantum chemistry
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this lesson, the student will be able to:
1.​ Describe fundamentals of quantum mechanics and its applications to chemistry
2.​ Solve and analyze exactly solvable problems and interpret solutions to discuss symmetry, energy
levels, spectroscopy, atomic orbitals and spins
Contents
The transition from classical to quantum regime, Uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation and its
physical interpretation, Time-independent Schrödinger equation, wave functions, operators, commutator
algebra and Uncertainty principle, Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors in quantum mechanics (10 lectures)
Particle in a one-dimensional box, Measurement outcomes and Fourier series, Postulates and theorems in
quantum mechanics, Particle in a three-dimensional box- separation of variables, Wave functions and
symmetry in quantum mechanics, Finite square well and tunnelling (10 lectures)
Classical Harmonic oscillator, The Harmonic oscillator model for a diatomic molecule and its relation to
infrared spectra, Vibrations of diatomic molecules, Harmonic oscillator selection rules (9 lectures)
The rigid-rotator model for a diatomic molecule, Angular momentum, Rigid-rotator selection rules, the
hydrogen atom solution and atomic orbitals, Introduction to electron spin-Stern-Gerlach experiment,
Zeeman effect and spin-orbit coupling, Many-electron systems (10 lectures)
Lab Experiments: 1] Determination of lambda max and calculation of transition energy by UV-visible
spectroscopy, 2] Determination of force constant of a diatomic molecule using IR, 3] proton NMR spectra
of acetone, 4] Calculation of extinction coeffciient using Beer Lambert’s Law, 5] Effect of solvent polarity
on emission spectra, 6] Plotting wave functions using Mathematica.
Textbooks
1.​ Levine, I. N., (1983), Quantum Chemistry, 3rd Edition, Allyn and Bacon​
Reference Books
1.​ McQuarrie, D. A., (1983), Quantum Mechanics, 2nd Edition, University Science Books
2.​ Atkins, P. and Friedman (2005), R., Molecular Quantum Mechanics, 4th Edition, Oxford University
Press, London

Course_Title:
Objectives
1. To provide fundamental aspects of Thermodynamics, chemical equilibria and phase equilibria
Learning Outcomes
The students will be able to:
1. Describe thermodynamics, chemical equilibria and phase equilibria
2. Demonstrate the conductivity measurements
Contents
Thermodynamics: Work, heat & energy, First Law of Thermodynamics, Enthalpy, heat capacity,
Expansion of ideal gas, Joule-Thomson effect, Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics, changes of enthalpy
and entropy in reactions, second law of thermodynamics, spontaneous, irreversible and cyclic process,
Carnot theory, entropy changes in various processes, Maxwell’s relations, Gibbs-Helmholtz equation,
thermodynamics of open system, chemical potential, Third law of thermodynamics, determination of
absolute entropies, entropy of real gas, residual entropy (15 lectures)
Chemical Equilibrium: Spontaneous reactions, Standard free energy, law of mass action, Van’t Hoff
reaction isotherm, De Donder treatment, chemical affni ity, Homogeneous equilibria, Temperature and
Pressure dependence of equilibrium constant, Van’t Hoff equation, Heterogeneous equilibria,
Equilibrium constant for reaction involving real gases (5 lectures)
Phase Equilibrium: Phase, Components, Degree of freedom, Gibbs phase rule, One-component
systems, High pressure phase diagrams, Two-component systems, Liquid-liquid and liquid-solid
equilibria, Eutectic systems, Thermal analysis, Cooling curves, Freezing point diagrams with
Congruent and incongruent melting, Three-component solid-liquid systems, Ehrenfest classifciation
of phase transitions. (10 lectures)
Electrochemistry: Faraday’s law, Types of conductance, Measurement of equivalent conductance,
Variation of conductance with dilution, Kohlrausch’s law, Arrhenius theory of electrolyte dissociation,
Weak and strong electrolytes, Ostwald’s dilution law, Debye-Huckel-Onsager’s equation for strong
electrolytes, Migration of ions, Transport number, Determination of degree of dissociation, ionic
product of water and solubility product of sparingly soluble salts, Conductometric titrations. (9
lectures)
Lab Experiments:
1] Determination of phosphoric acid content in soft drink using pH sensor and titrimetric analysis,
2] potentiometric titration of ferrous ammonium sulphate using KMnO4,
3] Estimation of free alkali present in soaps,
4] Determination of PI of amino acid using pH meter,
5] Conductometric titration of a strong acid by strong base, 6] Determination of CMC using
conductometric titration.
Textbook
1. Atkins, P.W.; Paula, J.de. (2014), Atkin’s Physical Chemistry Ed., 10th Edition, Oxford University
Press.
2. Levine, R. N. Physical Chemistry, sixth Ed., Mc Grow Hill
3. Ball, D. W. (2017), Physical Chemistry, 2nd Edition,Cengage Learning, India.
4. Castellan, G. W. (2004), Physical Chemistry, 4th Edition, Narosa.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The instructor will:
1. teach basic aspects of isolation and purifciation techniques, spectroscopic methods, important
analytical tools in academic research, chemical and pharmaceutical industries for isolation and
identifciation of organic molecules.
2. teach elucidation of structures of organic compounds using in-depth analysis of different
spectroscopic data.
3. provide a practical knowledge of organic chemistry.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
1.determine the structures of known/unknown organic molecules utilizing several spectroscopic
techniques mentioned in the content.
2. carry out simple synthetic organic transformations, isolate, purifciation and characterization of the
reaction products
3. be familiarized with physical data (melting point, boiling point, falsh point, etc.), toxicity, health
effects, reactivity, storage, disposal, and spill-handling procedures.
Contents
Purifciation Techniques: Crystallization, steam and vacuum distillation, fractional distillation,
sublimation, differential extraction, thin layer chromatography (TLC), column chromatography, HPLC
(3 lectures)
Infrared Spectroscopy: Introduction to IR spectroscopy, Modes of stretching and bending, stretching
frequencies of different organic functional groups, Effects of structural and conformational
environment (3 lectures)
Ultraviolet-Visible Spectroscopy: Studies on conjugated and extended conjugated systems, analysis
and interpretation of UV-Visible spectroscopic data, Application in mechanistic studies (3 lectures)
Mass Spectrometry: Principles of mass spectrometry, Different ionization techniques (EI, CI, ESI etc.),
GC-MS, HRMS, LC-MS and MS-MS techniques, Fragmentation and rearrangement of different classes
of organic molecules, Isotope effects, Identifciation of known/unknown organic compounds (6
lectures)
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy: Chemical shifts of different organic functional groups in
1H and 13C NMR, origin and interpretation of coupling constant, introduction to the principle and
interpretation of DEPT, COSY, NOESY, NOE techniques, Structural elucidation of organic compounds
(14 lectures)
Identifciation and Mechanistic Studies: Application of all above techniques in the structural
elucidation of unknown organic compounds and investigation of organic reaction mechanisms (10
lectures)
Lab Experiments:
1] Melting point measurement of a given organic compound;
2] Identifciation of an organic compound by HRMS;
3] Identifciation of functional group present using IR spectroscopy;

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
1.​ Give better insight into chemistry of main group elements and bioinorganic chemistry
2.​ Provide broad knowledge about properties and applications of compounds of main group
elements and metal ions essential in biological systems.
Learning Outcomes
The students are expected to have the ability to:
1.​ Appreciate chemistry of elements essential in biological systems.
2.​ Understand structure and bonding concepts in chemistry of s- and p-block elements and
systematic understanding of their chemical reactivity
Contents
Chemistry of main group elements: Molecular Geometry and Symmetry, hypervalency, Synthesis,
structure and bonding in polyhedral boranes and carboranes, Wade’s Rules, electron count, Isolobal
analogy. B-N, P-N, S-N unit containing compounds. Compounds of Silicon, Zeolites. Hydrides, halides,
oxides, nitrides of s- and p- block elements. Allotropes of Carbon, introduction to carbenes and their
heavier analogues. Chemistry of halogens and Noble gases, Chemistry of s-block elements.
Organometallic compounds of main group elements. (15 Lectures)
Spectroscopic Characterization: NMR, FT-IR, Raman, Mass etc. (4 Lectures)
Applications of main group compounds: Frustrated Lewis pairs and small molecule activation,
Synthetic uses of main group complexes, Oxidizing/reducing agents. Precursors for materials
deposition. Deposition of thin flims of materials, with a strong focus on Chemical Vapour Deposition
(CVD) and ALD. PET and SPECT imaging. (8 Lectures)
Bioinorganic Chemistry: Transition metals in biology - their occurrence and function, active- site
structure, Metalloenzymes; O2 binding properties of heme (hemoglobin and myoglobin) and
non-heme proteins hemocyanin & hemerythrin), co-operativity effect, Bohr Effect; representative
synthetic models of heme and nonheme systems. Electron transfer proteins - active site structure and
functions of ferredoxin, rubredoxin and cytochromes, and their comparisons. Metals in medicine. (12
Lectures)

Course_Title:

in the synthesis of natural products and pharmaceuticals.

Students will be able to:
1.​ Understand the basic heterocyclic principles and apply different types of organic reactions in
the synthesis of small heterocyclic compounds.
2.​ Learn the applications of modern organic synthetic tools in the effciient synthesis of
heterocycles.

Course_Title:
Objectives
The Instructor will:
1.​ Introduce a few spectroscopic methods used as analytical techniques in various feilds of
science and engineering.

Course Objectives
●​ Generate an idea of theatre: its history, aesthetics, social signifciance and contemporary practice
●​ Understand the signifciance of theatre as a medium for education and introduction to
contemporary theatre-in-education practices
●​ Develop basic knowledge and skills in script-writing, acting, blocking, stage design, sound design,
light design, costume design and production management
●​ Enhance confdi ence, communication, coordination, teamwork and presentation skills through
collaborative theatre practice
Learning outcomes
●​ Knowledge of theatre as an art form: history, aesthetics and social signifciance
●​ Understand theatre’s importance as a medium for education
●​ Acquire practical knowledge and basic skills in script-writing, acting, stage design, sound design,
light design, costume design and production management
●​ Develop confdi ence, creativity, coordination, adaptability, and problem-solving aptitude through
immersive theatrical experiences
Course Contents
Topic 1: Introduction to Theatre and its role in Education (5 Lectures)
An overview of theatre history, different forms/genres of theatre globally and the power of performative
storytelling. Introducing the different elements of theatre making and the roles designed to manage
these different elements. Understanding the signifciance of theatre as a medium for education and
knowledge of contemporary theatre-in-education practices.
Topic 2: Script-writing and Dramaturgy (2 Lectures & 6 Studio Hours)
Different kinds of dramatic plots and structures will be analyzed and discussed. Understanding concepts
related to preparing the performance text: playwriting, character-development, plot-design, editing,
adaptation and incorporating stage directions. Students will write or adapt a short stageable dramatic
piece in groups.

Different approaches to acting will be analyzed and discussed with special emphasis on Stanislavsky’s
method. Concepts like ‘character-analysis' , ‘emotional memory’, ‘gestus’, ‘psycho-physical acting’ will be
introduced. Students will learn various skills like voice projection/modulation, play-reading, dialogue
delivery, recitation, facial and physical gestures, movements and coordination. The students will analyze
a given character and develop methods to enact the character.
Topic 4: Theatre Design (4 Lectures & 6 Studio Hours)
Understanding different aspects of theatrical design including direction, stage-design, light-design and
sound-design. Students will learn various concepts and practical techniques relating to theatrical design.
They will work hands-on in groups to formulate a design for a given dramatic piece.
Topic 5: Collaborative Production (10 Studio Hours)
